items.title: Man found dead in Queensland flood waters as state hit by multiple storms and days-long deluge
paragraphs: A man’s body has been found in flood waters following an unusual weather system that delivered multiple storms and a days-long deluge to parts of Australia.
Emergency services were called to a creek at Boompa on Queensland’s Fraser Coast shortly after 11am on Monday after reports a man had been found unresponsive.
The man was declared dead after being found in Smothering Creek on Boompa Road, Queensland police said.
An investigation into his death has begun, with police to prepare a report for the coroner.
Further south, six campers were rescued after becoming stranded by flood waters at a public campground in Leyburn in Queensland’s Southern Downs.
Queensland Fire and Rescue Swiftwater crews responded to the call for help at 7.45am on Monday.
They rescued three men aged 71, 47 and 26 and two women aged 68 and 26 without incident at about 11.15am.
There were no reports of physical injuries, Queensland police said in a statement.
Torrential downpours across Queensland between Thursday and Monday left many rivers and roads flooded across the state’s south and east.
There are warnings of more rain and flooding to come.
Flash flooding hit Laidley Creek and Glenore Grove in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane, closing some roads, Queensland police said on Monday.
The highest recorded four-day totals were spread across the state, with Blackdown Tableland, near Rockhampton, recording 439.4mm to early Monday.
Lower Springbrook, near the Gold Coast, recorded 325.2mm, while Nambour, near the Sunshine Coast, copped 314.2mm.
Brooweena, inland of K’gari, received 299.6mm.
Meteorologist Angus Hines said the system behind the downpours was unusual.

“The widespread rain bands with heaps of cloud cover, much cooler temperatures, and then the storms in that situation are really driven by what’s going on in the higher parts of the atmosphere,” he said.
On Sunday evening, thunderstorms were briefly connected from southern Queensland to Bass Strait, as a swift-moving system passed towards Australia’s east coast.
The storm band raced over most states, propelled by strong winds in the upper atmosphere.
“But that steering wind sort of just tapered off through the night last night over [Queensland’s] Darling Downs,” Hines said.
Flood warnings are current for Warrill Creek and the Bremer River in the Lockyer Valley, the Macintyre and Moonie rivers in the south, and the Mary River near the Sunshine Coast.
Western Queensland also remains on alert, with warnings current for the Warrego River at Charleville, the Bulloo River in Quilpie, and the Barcoo River at Blackall.
The Bureau of Meteorology said Queensland’s weather was set to return to more typical spring conditions as the week continued.
Hot and humid days are expected to give way to more subdued afternoon showers and storms.

items.title: China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in Party
paragraphs: Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past Plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.

According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This Plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

items.title: UK poised to miss reduced aid spending target of 0.3% of national income
paragraphs: The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year.
Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027.
The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income.

However, they said it was “very plausible” that the shortfall would be £580m, at only 0.28% of national income. Even the most conservative forecast implies a £250m shortfall, according to the estimates.
Ian Mitchell, a senior fellow at the CGD and co-director of its Europe programme, described these as “material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid”.

Making up a shortfall of even £400m would be enough to halve cuts to Africa that are likely to cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de facto exit from the south and east of the continent, he said.

The CGD attributed the shortfall to higher than expected inflation, which means national income will be higher than forecast at the spending review, and a 2025 policy change around the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) budget.
The researchers called on ministers to consider allocating additional funds to international aid in this week’s budget, to avoid the embarrassment and criticism from missing a target.
The 0.3% spending target for 2027 is far below the 0.7% promised in Labour’s election manifesto, having been downgraded by Keir Starmer to boost spending on defence.
Fleur Anderson, a former minister who sits on the foreign affairs select committee, said she would like to see higher spending on development aid in the budget.
She said: “I’d like to see this government going further and reversing these cuts altogether in time, but at the very least we should be hitting the reduced target that was set.
“Falling short isn’t an abstract accounting issue. It means communities not having clean water, girls pulled out of school, vaccines that don’t get delivered, peace programmes in war zones cut.
“The upcoming budget presents real opportunity for the Treasury to address this and for the government to show that its words on Britain’s place in the world are matched by action.”
Charities have repeatedly said that the government’s deep aid cuts will hit children’s education and increase the risk of disease and death in some African countries.

The latest figures released by the FCDO in September showed that British aid cuts under Starmer’s government hit the world’s poorest countries the hardest, while higher-income countries’ share of aid increased. The data showed a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.
The UK’s overall official development assistance (ODA) budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income, compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m.

The government has prioritised spending through multilateral agencies such as the World Bank’s development arm, the International Development Association, and the global vaccines initiative Gavi. It has also continued to fund humanitarian support.

The Conservative party and Reform UK have pledged to slash aid even further, from about £9bn a year to £1bn – a level that would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank.

An FCDO spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.
“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”

items.title: Brazil keeps left: what Lula’s victory means for his country and beyond
paragraphs: Good morning. Chances are you woke this morning to news of two momentous election results. In Serbia, a student-led movement has ousted the country’s long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vučić (which you can read more about here). And just hours ago, Brazil’s president staged a sensational turnaround against his far-right opponent after a nail-biting vote.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, won a forth nonconsecutive term as president, seeing off far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who spearheaded the radical populist movement built by his father and former president, Jair. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election.

After Bolsonaro’s surprise first-round victory earlier this month, the Workers’ party incumbent Lula pulled off a historic fightback – a consolidation of the democratic resurgence the country has enjoyed since he took office – and an early birthday present for the veteran leftist, who turns 81 on Tuesday.

But with Bolsonaro refusing to accept the result, the victory is a tense one. I spoke to the Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips, who was in São Paulo at the Workers’ party vote count, to find out what the result means and what may lie ahead.
UK news | Two people have been killed and more than 160,000 properties have been left without power as Storm Boelo continues to batter the UK.
Crime | British police are recording a growing number of crimes linked to cocaine, including assaults, domestic abuse and dangerous driving, as figures show consumption has surged across England.

France | Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.

UK politics | Prime minister Andy Burnham’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with Europe has been backed by senior cabinet ministers including Angela Rayner but risks causing concern among fellow red wall MPs.
Aviation | Three in four European airline pilots have taken microsleeps in the cockpit, while almost a quarter routinely fly despite being too fatigued to work, according to a report.

When the results were declared just after midnight UK time, the choice of Brazil’s 159 million voters was narrow, but clear. The 80-year-old leftist received 51.79% of the vote to his rival’s 48.21% – about 4.3m votes – in what Lula called “a defeat for denialism”.
A visibly angry Bolsonaro has already refused to concede, citing a decision to extend voting for an extra two hours – although both sides had called for it, for different reasons.
The outcome was an unprecedented turnaround after a populist surge in first-round voting at the beginning of the month left Brazil’s progressives reeling.

In those early October elections, Flávio Bolsonaro received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – putting the 45-year-old scion of the authoritarian clan in pole position: not once, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.
In the intervening weeks, the polls tightened dramatically, putting Bolsonaro ahead by only fractions of a percentage point.

“This is the crescendo of an incredible, if sometimes controversial, 50-year political career,” Tom says. I can hear crowds of Lula supporters cheering in the background as we speak, and fireworks exploding. “It saw Lula go from rural poverty to union leader to the first elected working-class leader of Brazil, who has helped millions of people escape poverty and rode a commodities boom in his first two terms”.

For Brazil, a Lula win represents stability and the assurance that the country’s democratic future is secure, at least in the short term. “Over the past four years, Lula has reduced deforestation in the Amazon by more than 70%. He’s come to the help of the Indigenous people who live there. He’s cracked down on illegal mining,” Tom tells me. “It’s very positive news is that all this will continue.”

“Bolsonarismo is a far-right movement … that has put down deep roots in Brazilian society,” Bernardo Mello Franco, a political columnist for the Rio broadsheet O Globo, told Tom earlier this month, pointing to a series of societal shifts have contributed to this.
Evangelical Christianity has expanded across Brazil in recent decades, with church leaders throwing their support behind the socially conservative policies favoured by Bolsanaro Sr and Jr.

Pro-gun Flavio Bolsonaro harnessed voter frustration at chronic levels of urban crime and violence. Despite being embedded in Brazilian politics for decades, he successfully portrayed himself as an anti-establishment outsider, using social media far more effectively than his rival.

And others believe he had significant help: a dozen watchdogs and research groups have published reports alleging that Meta may have favoured the senator’s campaign. The controversy grew after Brazils’ electoral court ordered Meta not to give the candidates “unequal treatment”, while the company called the allegations “false and unfounded”.

Progressives were galvanised after the first-round results revealed a record abstention rate of 21%, more common among Lula-supporting groups such as lower-income voters, and their focus sharpened on mobilisation. Millions joined a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s army”, which sent out daily instructions on how to make supportive content go viral. The 80-year-old incumbent, who only took ownership of his first smartphone in recent days, started posting to Instagram and TikTok. For the first time, the president’s digital reach overtook that of Bolsonaro.

Meanwhile, the Bolsonaro campaign was hit by a succession of scandals. In a revelation that made the UK’s partygate seem tame by comparison, last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of the 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party along with sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to cut deals with his father’s government.

Amid speculation that a comeback might be possible, at a million-strong rally on Copacabana beach in Rio on Saturday, activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “We are going to turn this around!”
What role did Trump play in the election?

The US president has boasted about “lots of people that I got elected” in Latin America, styling himself as a kingmaker after a succession of right-wing candidates aligned with Washington have won power.

Although Donald Trump did not openly endorse Flávio Bolsonaro, his influence loomed large. Last year, he denounced the supreme court trial of his ally Jair Bolsonaro as a “witch-hunt”, imposing extraordinary 50% tariffs on Brazilian imports as retribution for what he claimed was political persecution.

Lula has styled himself as the country’s defender against Trump’s “colonial” designs. His victory consolidates a multilateral foreign policy and pragmatic approach to relations with the US, China and Russia. He has rejected invitations to join the controversial coalition of Latin American countries conducting military operations against drug cartels alongside the Pentagon, which would have resulted in much greater US involvement on Brazilian soil.

Furthermore, a win for pro-democracy campaigners in one country may serve to bolster international counterparts. As our senior international correspondent Julian Borger sets out in this compelling piece, along with the Brazil vote, a series of high-stakes elections in Serbia yesterday, Israel on Tuesday and the US next week are closely interlinked, and Lula’s win may have global ramifications, as leaders across Latin America and the world congratulate him this morning.
What does the result mean for the environment, in Brazil and beyond?

Last week, Tom travelled to Roraima, the northern state where Bolsonaro registered his best result nationwide. On his trip, he heard first-hand from Indigenous leaders and conservationists on why the populist’s success was causing panic.

His father’s environmentally devastating administration facilitated an illegal gold rush – turbo-charged by record global gold prices – that ravaged the Yanomami Indigenous reserve on the northern reaches of the Amazon.

When Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, the left-winger launched an environmentalist mission to expel the illegal miners, taking on the multibillion dollar extraction industry. Alongside wider green policies, he reduced deforestation in the Amazon to record lows.
“Tragically,” says Tom, “the environment only came up in the final presidential debate of this campaign.”

“Given that the Amazon makes up such a large portion of Brazil, and how important that region is to the global climate crisis, it’s amazing that it’s not been debated more. But people were voting more on economy, public security and culture war issues.”
In that final debate last Friday, Tom says that Lula “tried to show off the excellent, if incomplete, work that his government’s done in protecting the environment”.
Many will be relieved at Bolsonaro’s loss, as his vision for the Amazon was almost identical to his father’s.

While a Lula victory brings hope that these policies will continue, he will be working with a newly elected congress that features a record number of rightwing politicians hostile to Indigenous rights and environmental issues.
The immediate aftermath of the election results is likely to be fraught, warns Tom, with Flávio Bolsonaro saying it was “impossible to concede the election result”.

“The Bolsonaro response is exactly as I feared but I don’t think it will mean very much,” Tom says. “All these world leaders are now recognising Lula’s win and I don’t think Bolsonaro has a hope of overturning this result”.

Tom suspects that in the coming days Bolsonaro will head to the States, to avoid ongoing criminal investigations. “That’s not to say there might not be violence from his supporters, but his political career is done. The fact they’ve lost is a sign that the name ‘Bolsonaro’ is toxic for a slight majority of Brazilian people.”

Tuesday | Israel goes to the polls on Tuesday, amid orders from prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu for a full lockdown of the occupied West Bank after recent checkpoint attacks. His government will be fighting for its survival.

Wednesday | On Wednesday Chancellor John Healey will deliver his first budget statement in the House of Commons, which is expected to give local authorities more spending powers, as a means to promote growth

Thursday and Friday | European and Canadian leaders will meet in Montreal for the 21st EU-Canada summit, to discuss security and strategic cooperation. It will be the first opportunity for leaders to iron out details over a proposed invitation for Canada to become the EU’s first ever “associate member”

Greg Wise is bracingly open about his experience of IVF and how his struggle to conceive with his wife, fellow actor Emma Thompson, left him questioning his masculinity. Klara Kubiak, newsletters team
I enjoyed Ioan Marc Jones this morning, on how bell hooks revolutionised his worldview and got him to start telling the men in his life he loves them. Poppy Noor, acting head of newsletters
As someone who isn’t the biggest fan of feet, I found Chloe Mac Donnell’s piece about the current trend for ugly footwear equal parts fascinating and horrifying. Klara

I found Emma Beddington’s advice to teens wanting to know about the world of work – which includes the values of a pack of biscuits and realising that your boss sometimes just might be an idiot – in equal parts funny and wise. Poppy

Football | Manchester United’s hierarchy are in crisis talks over whether or not to sack Michael Carrick as head coach after he oversaw another torrid defeat, against Bournemouth at Old ­Trafford on Sunday, that left his job in the balance.
Formula One | The 20-year-old Kimi Antonelli won from Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen and should become F1’s youngest world champion next week in Mexico
Cricket | Shadab Khan made an unbeaten 113 in a thrilling last-wicket stand with Haris Rauf as Pakistan, chasing 242, beat England in a thriller
“‘Red Wall’ MPs wary as Burnham calls for EU free movement debate”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while Metro writes “Get Brexit Redone”.

The i Paper has “Streeting vows UK will ‘lead from the front’ as billions planned for defence boost”, the Times writes “Budget set to offer tax reprieve for pensioners” while the Express says “PM’s betrayal may ‘open door’ to EU migrants”.

Elsewhere, the Telegraph has “BBC’s £400k payout over anti-Semitism” and the FT has “Luxury houses shed €250bn in value as China’s shoppers tighten their belts”. The Mirror leads on “Meghan Dad ‘net will widen’” and the Mail has “Markle ‘abuser of worst kind’”.
How Abu Dhabi bought Andy Burnham’s Manchester
Today in Focus presenter and city resident Helen Pidd walks through modern Manchester – where Burnham was mayor for nearly a decade – and charts its transformation wrought by Emirati money.

Helen talks to North of England editor Josh Halliday too about how Abu Dhabi came to Manchester, alleged “sweetheart deals” it struck to own so much land, and a lack of transparency about it all even now.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Every autumn, Corvo Island in the Azores turns off its public lighting for a few key days to help fledgling seabirds fly to the ocean guided by the stars.

Since 2019, the 450 or so inhabitants of the smallest and most northerly island of Portugal’s Azores archipelago have switched off the lights for five nights to tackle the disastrous effects of artificial light on Cory’s shearwaters. The campaign started after the community noticed huge numbers of deaths among young shearwaters, who spend three months in their nests before attempting their first flight to the ocean. Many are fatally confused by the artificial glow of streetlights, and end up crashing on the streets of the island’s only village, Vila do Corvo. By going dark, the stars can be seen clearly, allowing the juvenile birds safe passage to the ocean.
And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

items.title: Angus Taylor criticised for ‘tone deaf’ response to alleged attack on Helen Haines
paragraphs: Angus Taylor has been criticised for his response to the alleged attack on Helen Haines, with crossbenchers Monique Ryan and Zali Steggall labelling a speech by the opposition leader “tone deaf” and saying he did not “read the room”.

Parliament returned in Canberra on Monday, a week after an alleged attack outside the Indi MP’s northern Victorian electorate office, which led to her losing both legs. A 43-year-old man has been charged and the incident continues to be investigated.
Former Liberal leader Peter Dutton told News24 he believed more violence against politicians was “inevitable” in Australia. Police have not revealed any established motive for the Haines attack.
“It came as no surprise to me, I am sorry to say. I think it has been building for a long period of time,” he said on Monday.
The episode has sparked debate about the safety of MPs and the state of the political environment, including the culture of parliamentary debates.
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, and the One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce have rejected calls for a change in practice to cool Australia’s political debate.
“In the past week, it has been suggested by some there is a causal connection between robust parliamentary debate and political violence,” Taylor said. “I disagree with this view.
“The Westminster system is about settling differences through robust and rigorous debate, not violence.

“Importantly, we debate with adversarial vigour, but we never allow that vigorous parliamentary debate to spill over into violence. People who resort to intimidation and violence cross a line that must never be crossed.”

He said Labor had been correct to call out far-right extremism in Australia but called for all extremism to be rejected. He said judges should “come down harder” on people found guilty of intimidation or violence.
“Another thing we must do is celebrate Australia more readily. Too many Australians have been taught to feel guilty and shame about our country and about our history.
“Is it any wonder that some feel deep animosity towards our democracy, our institutions, and our nation?”
Joyce told News24 his thoughts and prayers remained with Haines and her family, calling the alleged attack “so unAustralian”.

“Unfortunately what we’re seeing in Australia and around the world is a change in dynamics,” Joyce said. “I think parliament has got its part to play but I don’t think it’s going to be a solution to the problem.
“The issues, such as the Palestinian march across the [Sydney Harbour] Bridge, the vindictive, arsenic type of rhetoric that we see in the public realm, these are all part of it.
“I think it’s foolish to think if question time changes, Australia changes. Not necessarily, in fact highly unlikely.”
Steggall, the independent Warringah MP, who sits next to Haines in the lower house, said she was personally disappointed by Taylor’s speech.
“There is a link between our words and actions,” she said.
“I did not feel that Angus Taylor read the room when it comes to the lesson that Helen would like us all to learn.

“To make what’s happened to her, the utter tragedy of it, make sense to all of us, make sense for Australia, then we have to be able to take responsibility for the impact our words and our debate has beyond the walls of parliament.”
She said the same caution should be applied to media reporting, election advertising and social media posts.
Steggall referenced conversations with Haines’s husband, Phil Haines, in Canberra on Monday.
“His words to us, asking us to raise the bar so that when Helen does come back to this place, there’s been a meaningful shift in how we can have a respectful debate,” she said.
“We can disagree respectfully, but words matter and have an impact.”
Ryan, the Kooyong independent, called Taylor’s response “tone deaf” and “hugely disappointing”.
“If Angus Taylor doesn’t think that the words that we use matter, I don’t understand how he aspires to lead a political party,” she told ABC TV.
“If we can’t rise to the occasion now after something as unthinkable as what happened to Helen and think about how we behave in the house and in the public space … we’re never going to do that.”

items.title: Plans to create a wildflower meadow take shape
paragraphs: The authority said the wildflower meadow project, which followed the introduction of green hay in the area earlier this year, was one of its first practical initiatives to protect and restore habitats for insects and other wildlife across the borough.

Chris Walker, the biodiversity officer at the borough council, said: "We will be able to take what we learn from this project to recreate wildflower meadows in other areas of the borough, fitting in with our long-term investment in nature."
Wildflower meadows are among the UK's most valuable habitats, external, supporting a wide range of insects and wildlife while helping to connect fragmented natural spaces.
The council said once fully established, the Fairstead Recreation Ground meadow would provide food, shelter and breeding opportunities for numerous species.

It added it would continue to monitor the site's progress as the meadow develops, with the aim of creating a self-sustaining habitat to support biodiversity and potentially provide seed and plant material for future meadow creation projects elsewhere in the borough.

items.title: Daughter wins £127k claim for caring for mum at home
paragraphs: Bern says her mother wanted to be cared for at home by her family
ByMatty EdwardsBristol and Fiona LamdinWest of England home and social affairs correspondent
A woman has described her "phenomenal" relief after she won a legal case that means she is entitled to be paid for caring for her elderly mother in her final years.
Bern Rogers, from Bristol, told the BBC of the "harrowing and deeply sad" family dispute since her elderly mother Sheila died in 2020, which even led to her facing criminal charges.
Legal experts said the "hugely significant" High Court ruling would lead to other claims.

The executor of Sheila's estate, Bern's brother Andrew, said it had "always been willing to pay" her "genuine expenses" and an extra amount for her efforts. But the estate intends to appeal against the judgment that awarded Bern £127,500 for care she provided.
Bern looked after Sheila, who had dementia, for two-and-a-half years.
After Sheila moved into Bern's house in Bristol in September 2017, she wanted to be cared for by her daughter rather than get costly home care or go into a residential care home.
Crucially, Bern said she agreed with her mother she would be paid for the round-the-clock care.
After Sheila died in April 2020, Bern took £100,000 from her estate. It led to her being reported to the police for fraud and theft.
The money was seized and Bern was charged. But, at a trial at Bristol Crown Court in 2022, she was found not guilty by a jury.
After being cleared, Bern turned to the civil courts.
In 2025, a High Court judge ruled she had entered into an informal contract with Sheila for payment of a reasonable sum for her care.
The estate was also ordered by a judge to pay Bern's legal costs.
In August this year, another High Court judge worked out the amount Bern was due and ruled she was owed £127,500 for the 850 days of care she provided.
Sheila was diagnosed with dementia after moving in with her daughter
"Mum came to live with me, she became very confused and was seen wandering in the garden and obviously needed care," Bern said. "We didn't know what was wrong with her."
She said caring for her mother had been like a full-time job, adding: "I couldn't leave her really. She became unpredictable."
Sheila became more frail, was diagnosed with dementia and also had a series of physical health problems, including a "chronic" and "disabling" prolapse.
Bern's husband John said: "It was relentless after she moved in with us. We couldn't go out even to the shops. It was a 24-hour job.
"It was a privilege, but we had to put our lives on hold for more than two years and revolve our lives around looking after her."
He remembered that in Sheila's final weeks, his wife was sleeping on the floor of her mother's bedroom to make sure she was alright.
Bern said "of course" she would have looked after her mother if she had not been able to pay her.
But she said her mother had wanted to be looked after by her daughter rather than getting professional carers or going into a home, which would have cost thousands of pounds a month.
"She was very insistent and would tell anyone that would listen that she wanted to make sure that I sorted out money for her care, I was to make sure I got paid properly," she said.
Multiple messages from Bern's five siblings were shown in court saying that she should be paid something for the care, although no amount was agreed.
That is why, she explained, shortly after her mother had died, she transferred £100,000 from her mother's account.
Bern was reported to the police for theft and fraud, which she describes as a "terrible and devastating betrayal".
"It has been harrowing and deeply sad for it to go from a normal family relationship to being treated like a scapegoat, five against one," she said.
Bern Rogers says she and her husband John can get on with their lives now after the two High Court rulings
After the two separate High Court judgements in her favour, Bern said: "The weight off my shoulders was phenomenal.
"It has been absolutely wonderful to be vindicated. It means I can get on with my life now, the rest of my retirement."
John said: "I'm very proud of her, actually, because she has stuck up for her mother, for carers and for herself.
"It's been a very long and tough journey of nine years, and we've finally got justice."
Legal experts have told the BBC that while this case does not automatically set a legal precedent, it is likely to lead to similar claims in future.

Emma Holland, partner in trust and litigation at Stewarts, said: "What this case demonstrates is that the courts are willing to apply ordinary contractual principles to family relationships, which wasn't clear before."
This means family members are more likely to be entitled to payment if there is an informal agreement, she said, even without an amount being agreed.
"These are considered, well-reasoned judgements by highly esteemed judges, so I would think it's very likely that future courts will follow them," Holland said.
Beth Middleton, senior associate in private wealth and disputes at JMW, said this was a "hugely significant" case that would "open a floodgate of claims".
Sarama Dutton, partner at Collyer Bristow, who specialises in trusts, inheritance and wills, said the judgements were likely to be "influential".

"It demonstrates a willingness to look beyond individual care tasks and acknowledges the broader reality of providing care to an elderly relative, including the continuous supervision, responsibility and restrictions on personal freedom," she said.
Bern Rogers and her husband John say they feel pride that their ordeal could help other family carers in future
Bern said she was "terribly proud" that her case could influence others in future, which she said was her mum's "legacy".
"It's a huge win for carers everywhere," John added, but stressed families still needed to have open discussions about what was fair.
The ruling that states that Bern is entitled to payment cannot be appealed against, however, the estate intends to lodge an appeal against the second ruling that decided the amount owed.

The executor of Sheila's estate is Bern's brother, Andrew Wills. In a statement on behalf of the estate, he said: "The only agreements that we (her siblings) were aware of was for my mother to give Bernadette £50 per week 'keep' and to ensure that Bernadette was not to be out of pocket.
"We were not made aware of any other contract between our mother and Bernadette."
The statement added: "At all times I have attempted to be independent and to act in the best interests of the estate.
"The estate has always been willing to pay Bernadette her genuine expenses as well as an additional gratuity in recognition of her efforts for our mother.
"We have always tried to be fair. Unfortunately, our offers were not accepted by Bernadette who instead issued legal proceedings against the estate."

items.title: Kane, Yamal or Kvaratskhelia? BBC Sport pundits on who should win the men's Ballon d'Or
paragraphs: European football expert Julien Laurens: I think he was the best player in Europe last season, especially in the Champions League where he was outstanding. He helped lead the team to another title, a back-to-back one.

He got the penalty in the final, scored in both semi-finals, in the quarter-final, and in the last 16. He was amazing in those huge, huge games where you want your best players to step up. He deserves to win the Ballon d'Or for being the best player in the world all the way up to the World Cup.

He won't win it, unfortunately, because Lamine Yamal, for the player he is and how entertaining and spectacular he is, didn't really shine at the World Cup, even if Spain won it. He didn't really do that well in the Champions League for Barcelona, getting knocked out early. However, his style of football means he'll probably win it - but it should be Kvaratskhelia.

Ex-Liverpool and Blackburn full-back Stephen Warnock: I think it will be Lamine Yamal for helping Spain to win the World Cup. If you were asking who else is in the hunt, I would say Michael Olise, but my pick personally would be Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, he is unbelievable. I love watching him play. He had such an impact for Paris St-Germain and last season he was incredible. I just don't think he will get the votes with Georgia not being in the World Cup.

BBC Radio 5 Live Euro Leagues guest and Athletic reporter Rory Smith: It will probably go to Lamine Yamal because it generally goes to someone who has won the biggest trophy, and this is the World Cup. It shouldn't be him because he wasn't necessarily Spain's most important player but his fame and talent means it will be him.

Personally I would give it to Kvaratskhelia. He has been the most exciting player in European club football for a while now, a valuable part of the PSG team who retained the Champions League, and crucially I think you shouldn't suffer because you come from a country who isn't in the running to win the World Cup.

items.title: Weary driver creates AI 'litter-tracking dashcam'
paragraphs: A software developer became so frustrated by the amount of rubbish he saw dumped along roadsides that he built an AI-powered "litter dashcam" to expose the scale of the problem.
Robin Bennett, from Shrewsbury, developed the Roadside Litter app after noticing what he believed was a growing amount of litter while driving around the county.
The technology has already logged more than 3,000 litter reports in Shropshire and more than 28,000 across the UK.

He is now sharing the data with anti-litter campaign group Clean Up Britain in the hope it will encourage action, while Shropshire Council said it was exploring ways to improve litter management on some of the county's busiest roads.

Bennett, who runs a software company in Telford, said he found the amount of rubbish on local roads "really depressing" and wanted to understand whether the issue was unique to Shropshire or part of a wider national problem.
After approaching Clean Up Britain to ask how he could help, he went on to develop what he describes as a "litter dashcam" that records rubbish spotted from a vehicle.
"My software company's created an app, which essentially is a litter dashcam," he said.
"The app records the litter that it sees."
Mounted on a vehicle dashboard, the app automatically takes a photograph every 10 seconds, identifying visible litter and grading it against a national standard before uploading the information.
Bennett said: "I've got a phone holder stuck to the dashboard, I've put my phone in securely.
"I start it and that's it, you don't have to touch the screen, and the screen will go black in a minute so it's not distracting in any way.
"Every 10 seconds it takes a photo, it looks at the litter it can see by the side of the road and it grades it according to a national standard."
The app had recorded more than 3,000 reports in Shropshire and more than 28,000 nationwide, Bennett said.
He added litter was particularly common near convenience stores, fast-food outlets and motorway service stations.
"People pick up a bag of fast food and just throw the bag out the window," he added.

items.title: Eric Bauza, voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies aged 46
paragraphs: Eric Bauza, the voice artist behind Looney Tunes characters including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, has died aged 46.
A statement from the Emmy award-winning star's family posted on Instagram, external said he had died "suddenly".
Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme, and appeared in the recent release Forgotten Island.
Variety reports that the cause of death was hypertensive cardiovascular disease and that Bauza died at home on Sunday.
In a 2021 interview with NBC News, Bauza, who was born in Ontario and was of Filipino descent, said he grew up a huge fan of the Looney Tunes characters and used to copy the voices as a child.
"Looney Tunes transcends all languages and all cultures," he said, external. "It doesn't matter what part of the planet you're from. You get the comedy."
He voiced Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd and Foghorn Leghorn in 2021's Space Jam: A New Legacy before reprising those roles and that of Road Runner in Coyote vs. Acme.
He also played the part of Toad General in 2023's The Super Mario Bros. Movie and its sequel The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, the fifth highest-grossing film internationally this year.
Between 2022 and 2025, he won three Emmy awards for outstanding voice performance in a number of TV series.

In a statement reported by the Hollywood Reporter, external, Channing Dungey, the chairman of Warner Bros. Television Group and US Networks, said: "Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world.
"He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life."

items.title: The dump detectives on the trail of the fly-tippers
paragraphs: Anthony Horan (left) and Ashley Hanley (right) from North East Lincolnshire trace criminals who illegally dump waste
A discarded microwave, a mattress sodden by the rain and even a pile of used syringes. The reality of illegally dumped waste sits before me in a colossal mound next to the side of a motorway.
For the team I'm with, this is a jigsaw waiting to be pieced together and solved as they try to identify the criminal culprits.
It does not take long for Anthony Horan and Ashley Hanley from North East Lincolnshire Council to find answers within the mountain of waste on the side of the Brocklesby Interchange near Grimsby.
"I'm gobsmacked at the amount of evidence in this one," Anthony Horan, who works as a senior environmental health practitioner for the authority.
"I'm disgusted at the needles. I've never found this amount ever."
Numerous syringes, some used, were found strewn within the heap
A number of times during the interview we pause after spotting a syringe close to our feet. Some are hidden under items, others are in plain sight.
The team tells me this is exactly why they wear protective equipment.
Meanwhile, a picture starts to emerge as letters with different names and addresses - all miles outside the area - are fished out and photographed.
Horan tells me if evidence which identifies a person is found, they will be questioned.
If found liable, they could be fined if they have not properly undergone a "domestic duty of care".
"A lot of people think enviro-crime or fly-tipping is a victimless crime," Horan says. "It's not, there's many victims."
Horan says people often employ a "man with a van" to dispose of their waste, but frequently the person hired just dumps it.
If the waste is found dumped on private land, the owner will have to pay for its removal. Councils only pay if it is on public land.
The team say fly-tipping costs the council thousands of pounds
Wearing thick gloves, environmental enforcement officer Hanley continues to dig through the dump.
I ask him about rogue waste removers and his advice for people wanting to get rid of waste.
"I would advise people to take the right precautions, make sure that they're giving it to somebody who has a waste carriage licence," Hanley says.
"Make sure that you're taking it to a proper waste facility if you're doing it yourself," he adds.
The Environment Agency says waste criminals "scar our environment and communities".
It says: "Illegal waste dumping is a crime that costs the public purse £1bn a year. We know the challenges and are working hard to overcome them."
It encourages the public to report suspected waste crime to its incident hotline or via its website.
In August, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said fines for fly-tipping would increase from £300 to £5,000 and offenders could be given up to nine points on their driving licence.
Hull City Council's fixed penalty notice for fly-tipping is £1,000
Across the Humber Bridge, I meet Hull City Council's Streetscene team as they arrive at a fly-tip in the middle of a housing estate.
Under this authority, the fines for fly-tipping are higher at £1,000.
As teams drag mattresses and wooden planks onto the truck, they tell a similarly frustrated story.
"It's all over the city and now it's on the rise," says Mike, one of the men clearing the waste.
"We've got a job to do so we have to clear it and move on to the next fly-tip and do the same again."
Carl Wilson, the team manager, tells me this location is a hotspot and criminals will be back soon enough.
"This will all get cleared away and then in a couple of weeks they'll probably do it again," Carl says.
"That's why you need this evidence to catch them, to stop them, to put it to a stop."
The authority tells me they often visit hotspots to deliver letters to residents on how to properly dispose of waste to prevent fly-tipping.
Evidence is collected and photographed as part the investigation
Back near Grimsby, I ask the North East Lincolnshire team what their message is to fly-tippers or people considering dumping their waste.
"Don't do it because we'll catch you," he says. "We don't want to be doing this, we want you to do the correct thing."

items.title: Fire-hit nature reserve 'will never be the same'
paragraphs: A nature reserve has said the wildlife "will never really be the same again" after a huge wildfire almost three months ago.
The blaze, which broke out on 29 July, started on the edge of RSPB Minsmere before it spread to neighbouring Dunwich Heath on the Suffolk coast.
Firefighters have been unable to determine the cause.
Ian Barthorpe, visitor experience officer at Minsmere, said the team was concerned about the long-term implications the fire.
"It's going to be a long process of recovery of the habitat and some species like the deer and the birds have relocated to other parts of the reserve," he explained.
"But unfortunately we're really concerned about the impacts it will have on some of the invertebrates, the plants and the reptiles.
"It'll be 20 years or more before those parts of the reserve start to look like they used to."
Some trails and heathland areas of the site were hit by the fire, but fortunately wind conditions as well as the vegetation and marshland had stopped it spreading further into the reserve.
Parts of the heathland were still recording temperatures of more than 53C (127F) underground earlier this month.

items.title: A man attacks a politician in Australia – level 1
paragraphs: An Australian politician named Helen Haines is badly hurt. A man in a car attacks her outside her office. She loses a leg in the hospital.
The driver hits her on purpose. A local barber helps stop the driver. Police catch him. He is 43 years old. Australian leaders are very sad and shocked.
Haines is a kind person who works hard for her area. Australian Prime Minister asks people to stop using bad and angry words in politics. Many people wish Haines to get well soon.
Difficult words: on purpose (when you do something and you plan it before), barber (a person who cuts and styles people’s hair and men’s beards), shocked (very surprised and upset).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: A man attacks a politician in Australia – level 2
paragraphs: An Australian politician named Helen Haines is fighting for her life after a driver deliberately hit her with a car outside her office. She suffered severe injuries, and doctors had to amputate her leg.

A brave local barber stopped the driver and took away a knife he had before police arrested him. Police charged a 43-year-old man in connection with the attack. Australian Prime Minister condemned the attack and asked leaders to stop angry political language across the country. People know Haines as a popular politician who works closely with her local community. This terrible event shocked Australians and raised serious worries about safety for politicians who normally meet people easily in public.
Difficult words: deliberately (done on purpose), amputate (to cut off a part of the body), condemn (to openly say that you disagree with something).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: A man attacks a politician in Australia – level 3
paragraphs: Independent Australian lawmaker Helen Haines remains in critical condition following a shocking vehicle attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, Victoria.

A 43-year-old suspect allegedly rammed his car into her while she was standing near the trunk of her vehicle, and then backed up to strike her again. A local barber disarmed and held the suspect until police arrived. Authorities have charged the suspect, while counterterrorism units and federal police assist with the investigation. The attack resulted in the amputation of one of the woman’s legs, and surgeons are working to save her other leg.

Haines is known for her political integrity and independent work representing regional interests, and she is widely respected across party lines. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called the event a deliberate act and warned against growing hostility and rhetoric directed at elected officials. The incident has raised deep concerns about security and the changing safety of public access to politicians in Australia.

Difficult words: electorate office (an office maintained by an elected representative in their local district to serve and meet with local citizens), amputation (the surgical removal of a limb or part of the body), hostility (aggressive, unfriendly behavior or feelings towards someone), rhetoric (language used to influence people, often used in political debates).

items.title: Knighting Sinfield 'easiest decision anyone's had to make,' says Prince William
paragraphs: Watch: The Prince of Wales says Sir Kevin "binds and glues communities together"
The Prince of Wales has said awarding a knighthood to rugby league star Sir Kevin Sinfield "was probably the easiest decision anyone's ever had to make".
Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Prince William spoke about his personal admiration for Sir Kevin, who recently completed seven ultra marathons in seven days.
It was his latest endurance challenge to raise money for Motor Neurone Disease (MND) charities following the death of his friend and former team-mate, Rob Burrow, from the condition in 2024.
"I think frankly he should have been Sir Kevin years ago," said Prince William.
"What Kevin does, is he can bind and glue communities together by being that leader. The more Kevs we have in this country the better."
The Prince and Princess of Wales were in Wakefield in West Yorkshire last month to see for themselves just how gruelling the seven ultramarathon challenge was.
William and Catherine surprised Sir Kevin as he completed the third of the marathons.
"I don't know how he keeps going, I'm worried about his knees, I'm worried about his hips. The guy is just a machine," Prince William told the BBC.
Sir Kevin Sinfield was made a knight bachelor by the Prince of Wales at Windsor Castle in October 2026
"He's a top bloke, really nice guy, good, honest, kind, decent northerner and I love that about Kevin, that there is no ego with him. He is what you get."
Rob Burrow's MND diagnosis changed a relationship between team-mates into a public campaign to raise awareness.
Sir Kevin supported Rob and his family through the difficult progression of the disease, becoming an important fundraiser for the MND community.
"That lack of ego is really important in a world that everyone wants to show how amazing they all are… Kevin does it very quietly very subtly," explained the prince.
Prince William with Rob Burrow and Sir Kevin at the Headingley Stadium in Leeds, January 2024

Prince William also told BBC Breakfast about writing to Rob Burrow's wife, Lindsey, and children, Macy, Maya and Jackson, after Rob's death. He said he was in awe of how Lindsey had coped with such quiet dignity.
He wrote the letter as a member of the Royal Family but also as someone who understood the anguish of losing a parent.
"Everyone grieves differently and every circumstance is different so you need to take your time over it," he said. "It's always better to say something around grief than it is to ignore it."
In November last year, I watched Prince William officially open the Rob Burrow Centre for Motor Neurone Disease at Seacroft Hospital in Leeds alongside the Burrow family.
The facility is dedicated to medical and holistic patient care as well as research into the condition. It was a deeply moving day for everyone there - but one filled with optimism.
"It was very emotional actually and, for me, doing personal, emotional work is more fulfilling," the prince said.

"For Lindsey, Rob and the family to ask me to come up and open the centre was not only very personally rewarding for me but really important that that circle was closed, and I really wanted to honour that."

In the BBC Breakfast interview, the prince also praised the courage and impact of the Scottish rugby union player, Doddie Weir, who did so much to raise awareness of MND before his death from the disease in 2022.
And there was also additional praise for William's aunt, the Princess Royal Anne, who has supported the MND community for many years.
Royal duty can be formal, even distant at times, but the story of Rob Burrow, his family and his friend Sir Kevin has clearly made an impact on a future King.

"He's a very kind, caring, human being but he's still a lunatic. How he manages all these things I don't know. He's gold dust he really is… if you could bottle it up and sell it, it would be priceless."
Thank You Sir Kev, Monday 26 October BBC One 20:00 and on iPlayer

items.title: Think Architecture's fragmented House on a Slope overlooks Lake Zurich
paragraphs: A cluster of interconnected volumes in dark limestone and cedar gradually descend down a narrow and steeply sloping site overlooking Lake Zurich at House on a Slope by Swiss studio Think Architecture.
Designed to sit harmoniously within the surrounding terrain, the 1,000-square-metre private home is split into two distinct blocks connected by a “subterranean art corridor”.
“The brief was to bring a very large programme into a narrow, steeply sloping site with as much sensitivity as possible,” Think Architecture creative director Marco Zbinden told Dezeen.

“We were interested in the quiet rhythm of the neighbouring houses, their individual scale, and the way they sit within the landscape. Breaking the residence into smaller volumes allowed us to respond to that context without losing the generosity of the interior,” he continued.
“From the outside, the house feels less like a single monumental object and more like a group of familiar structures that have always belonged to the hillside.”
Intended to emulate the surrounding landscape, the lakeside home was divided into two blocks, a “family house above, and a more grounded, protective house for children and guests below”.

“They are intimately connected through a corridor – filled with art – and the central garden level, which becomes the social heart of the home,” said Zbinden. “There, the architecture opens up, materials continue from outside to inside, and the different parts of the family’s life naturally meet.”

The larger, upper block, which is entered at street level, contains all the main living spaces including the kitchen, living room and dining room. These spaces are arrange over the first and lower floors, with large cedar-clad-timber windows giving views down the hillside. Several bedrooms are located on the top floor.

The lower level of the home opens up to a garden and large pool with a planted roof terrace sitting on the roof of the lower block. Clad in dark-limestone, this lower block is more enclosed with additional bedrooms for the family.
Carefully positioned openings within both structures allowed for the planting of native trees, ensuring a seamless transition into the mature foliage of the hillside.
Think Architecture designed the upper interior spaces to be open and airy, while the spaces in the lower block were more enclosed and calm.
“The interiors were conceived as a direct continuation of the architecture, extending its material language into the most private and lived-in spaces,” said Zbinden.
“We worked with a limited palette of bog oak, cedar, oak, Belgian bluestone, terrazzo, and patinated brass. Materials that are tactile, honest, and become more beautiful as they age,” he continued.
“The aim was to create spaces that felt warm and enveloping rather than decorated: quiet rooms shaped by light, texture, and proportion, where one can truly slow down and feel at home.”

House with a Slope is the most recent addition to a number of homes overlooking Lake Zurich completed by Think Architecture in recent months, including a minimal hilltop home and a home next to a vineyard.

items.title: 'Why we think Milton Keynes can be a City of Culture'
paragraphs: Maureen Onwunali, who grew up in Milton Keynes, said that writing a poem to help launch its UK City of Culture bid helped her learn more about the place

Milton Keynes has often been dismissed as somewhere not worth pulling off the M1 for, frequently by people who have no plans on visiting in the first place. But recently, that tide has turned. The BBC spoke to four people who have been part of the city's evolution and believe it has a chance of being crowned the UK City of Culture for 2029.
In 2025, the city was named one of the best places to live and work in the UK.
It is now in with a real chance of winning the £10m prize having been shortlisted as one of four places for the City of Culture contest.
The shorthand used to describe Milton Keynes often refers to concrete cows and its many roundabouts.
However, for Irish-born Nigerian creative Maureen Onwunali, who grew up and lives here, the city has so much more to offer.
While researching for her poem as part of the city's original bid, she said she found it "surprisingly so fascinating".
"I devoured all of these facts so now at any party, I have at least five Milton Keynes facts."
In "An ode to Milton Keynes", Onwunali refers to "the colossus, the world's first programmable computer" and "self-driving cars on Roman roads".
She told the BBC: "It's so funny because I tell people about Milton Keynes and culture and they look at me as if I'm being sarcastic, because Milton Keynes has this stereotype of being soulless.
"But there's so many artists who've come out of Milton Keynes.
"A lot do go off to bigger cities like London or Manchester but I think it's just a matter of harnessing their talents and having opportunities to platform them."
Milton Keynes Gallery director Anthony Spira said people outside the city would be surprised to see it on the shortlist because of "negative external perceptions"

Cultural events already held in the city include Reggae Land at the National Bowl and the Milton Keynes International Festival. This is alongside annual functions held at Campbell Park such as Art in the Park, the Zimbabwe Heritage Festival, MK Pride and Oktoberfest.
On the day the shortlist was announced, a four-month exhibition celebrating the life of British artist Laurence Stephen Lowry opened at the MK Gallery.
Director Anthony Spira said it was "great" that the city's place on the shortlist had surprised people.
"People who live here absolutely love it. But externally, people are saying, 'Milton Keynes, is there culture there?' Well, yes, there is, there's a lot and there's going to be a lot more."
Spira is confident the city, which was born only 59 years ago, can win: "We've got a very different story."
Theatre director Rosemary Hill said the city already had a fantastic creative grassroots community
Alongside its gallery, the city is proud of its theatre and live music venue - The Stables - which was developed by world-renowned jazz musicians Sir John Dankworth and Dame Cleo Laine.
The city is also home to smaller creative groups.
The professional theatre company The Play's The Thing was set up by Rosemary Hill in 2008 and encourages new writers and performers as well as producing more traditional plays.
"We've got a fantastic grassroots community doing so many things," said Hill.
However Hill still finds herself having to convince others of her beloved city's charms.
She recalled: "I was sitting on a train a few years ago and was getting off at Milton Keynes and somebody said, 'Oh, this is a place best avoided'.
"I said, 'Have you ever been here? Do you know what Milton Keynes is about. Because you should come and visit and see all these different things.
"The whole carriage clapped as I got off."
Deputy council leader Lauren Townsend said her good friend Shanika Mahendran, who died in July, played a key part in the city making the shortlist
For Lauren Townsend, the deputy leader of Milton Keynes City Council, her connection with the bid is also personal.
Fellow Labour councillor Shanika Mahendran died after a short illness aged just 28 in July.
At her memorial service former council leader Pete Marland revealed she had been the lone voice in the council chamber who persuaded the authority to throw its hat in the ring.
Shanika Mahendran, who died aged 28 in July, persuaded her fellow councillors in Milton Keynes to bid for UK City of Culture

Townsend, who was born and raised in Milton Keynes, said: "Her ambition and belief in our city, combined with the overwhelming support from local people, businesses and organisations, has resulted in us making the final shortlist, and shows just how far our city has come over the past decade.
"I will forever be grateful to pioneers like Shanika for leading the way on a huge opportunity to shine a spotlight on everything that makes our city unique."
Milton Keynes is now one of four places in the running to become UK City of Culture for 2029
The UK City of Culture for 2029 will be announced in early 2027
Milton Keynes, like Wrexham in Wales which is also on the shortlist, was made a city in 2022 as part of the Queen's Platinum Jubilee celebrations.
They are competing with Sheffield and Blackpool with a panel of judges including Grange Hill, Brookside and Hollyoaks creator, Sir Phil Redmond, who will visit each one
Judges will use set criteria, external to decide the winner, which include how places will create transformative opportunities and richer lives, deliver good jobs and boost growth
Shortlisted cities each receive £125,000 to help with their final bids.
The winner gets a £10m prize. In Bradford, which is the current holder of the title, around 7,000 new jobs have been created, as well as a brand-new performance venue.
Milton Keynes makes shortlist for City of Culture
But it’s up against stiff competition from three other cities, as Sam Read reports.
