The award’s rigorous and transparent judging framework requires the 130-plus jury members to examine entries over two rounds of evaluations. According to iF Design, every entry receives a detailed feedback chart, regardless of award outcome.

The chart provides a breakdown of the jury’s scores across the five criteria, along with comparisons with other entries, offering objective insight into a project’s strengths and areas for improvement, backed by independent expert validation.

“We see the iF Design Award as one of the world’s most important design platforms where leading brands, start-ups, designers and creators can challenge themselves, be inspired and stand out from the competition,” said iF Design CEO Uwe Cremering.
For award recipients, that recognition carries particular significance, iF Design explained.

“Being part of this [award], surrounded by the very best in the industry, is both humbling and deeply inspiring,” said Christian Schluender, senior vice president, general manager of Global Design at Harman.
“We are truly honoured to be recognised among such an outstanding group of peers. This award means so much to us because of the calibre of the competition and the excellence it represents.”

The award’s international standing is evident in its illustrious list of former winners, which includes Spanish designer Patricia Urquiola, who received the iF Design Lifetime Achievement Award for 2026.
Last year, British architect Norman Foster was the recipient of the same award, following German industrial designer Dieter Rams in 2024.
A former iF jury member with longstanding ties to the organisation, Rams has also contributed to the iF Design Foundation’s research and initiatives on design education.

Winners of the iF Design Award 2026 also include The Grand Ring – a landmark wooden structure created for Expo 2025 Osaka by Japanese architect Sou Fujimoto, which received the Gold Award for architecture.

Meanwhile, the wireless Music Studio 5 speaker designed by Erwan Bouroullec for Samsung took home the Gold Award for product design. In 2025, the sculptural Haikou Gaoxingli Insun Cinema by One Plus Partnership was among the Gold Award winners for interior architecture.

Alongside the award, iF Design further advances design excellence and impact with its annual iF Design Trend Report, Trend Conference, and award-winning Future of XYZ interview series, while the recently launched iF Design Academy offers expert-led courses tailored specifically for design leaders.
“With the final deadline for the iF Design Award 2027 fast approaching, designers, studios and brands have one last opportunity to enter,” said iF Design.
“For those with exceptional projects deserving of international recognition, this is the final chance to have your work celebrated alongside some of the world’s most respected names in design.”
Entries to the iF Design Award 2027 close on 2 November 2026. To learn more and enter, visit ifdesign.com before the final deadline.

items.title: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope
paragraphs: Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her show-stopping second album This Music May Contain Hope.
A pop record sprinkled with golden age Hollywood glamour, it beat the likes of Sir Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean and Jade to scoop the £25,000 prize.
"I couldn't tell you how grateful I am to be holding this," said Raye, clutching her trophy at Newcastle's Utilita Arena. "I'm shaking, I'm jet-lagged, I'm tired. It's all blurry."
It is the first time a pop album has won the coveted prize - which recognises the best British or Irish album of the last 12 months - since M People's Elegant Slumming in 1994.
Speaking to the BBC afterwards, Raye said she'd "poured everything I had" into the record, which features the global hit song Where Is My Husband?
"I made this album not focusing on commercial [success], not focusing on making things cookie-cutter," said the 28-year-old.
"Some of these songs are seven minutes. They're indulgent. They're maximalist."

Across 17 tracks and 73 minutes, the record tells a cinematic story about a relationship that ends in tears on the rainy streets of Paris, then follows our plucky heroine as she dusts off the debris and emerges stronger and more resilient.
Along the way, it features both of her grandparents, the soul legend Al Green, four separate orchestras and more than 100 musicians.
In the run-up to this year's ceremony, Olivia Dean had been the bookmakers' favourite for her second album, The Art of Loving.

An easy-going, soulful collection of love songs, it had already been named album of the year at the Brit Awards and the Mobos, and is widely expected to earn the singer a Grammy nomination in the same category next month.
Speaking backstage, the singer said she was overwhelmed by the success.
"I don't think I've processed it yet, to be honest," she said. "I feel like I'm still in this crazy whirlwind of it all.
"And maybe, when I take a break over Christmas, I'll reflect on the sofa."
Other nominees included the rapper Kojey Radical, Geordie jazz act Knats, and former Little Mix star Jade - who was the first ever X Factor winner to receive a Mercury nomination.

The shortlist also included the charity compilation album Help (2), recorded in aid of Warchild, which featured new music and cover versions by artists such as Olivia Rodrigo, Damon Albarn, Depeche Mode and The Last Dinner Party.
The tracklist also included nine former Mercury Prize winners: Arctic Monkeys, Young Fathers, Wolf Alice, Pulp, Sampha, Portishead's Beth Gibbons, Arlo Parks, English Teacher and Ezra Collective.
Last year, the prize was won by Newcastle singer-songwriter Sam Fender, who donated his £25,000 winnings to grassroots music venues, helping to support up-and-coming songwriters around the UK.

items.title: Call of Duty promises a return to form - but can it compete with GTA?
paragraphs: Call of Duty is back - and it's got a lot to prove.
Last year was a low point for the video game juggernaut, with poor reviews for its single-player campaign mode and multiplayer fans defecting to rival titles.
So for latest instalment, Modern Warfare 4, publisher Activision is pulling out all the stops to bring fans back on board.
But with increasing competition for fans' time and attention, and the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 just weeks away, can Call of Duty still cut through?
BBC Newsbeat spoke to some of those behind the game to find out, and why they see the upcoming release of GTA 6 as an "opportunity".
Since 2009, Call of Duty has been at the top - or a close second-place - in the US video game sales charts every year.
But 2025's edition, Black Ops 7, dropped to seventh place in America, according to data from analytics firm Circana. In the UK, it was the eighth best-selling game, external.
It’s thought the game’s inclusion on Xbox’s Game Pass subscription service, where it won’t appear on release this year, hit sales.
But competition from long-running rival Battlefield 6 and new release Arc Raiders - a surprise success from Swedish studio Embark - put the behemoth on the back foot.
Fans also complained about the inclusion of novelty skins, which change the appearance of characters during multiplayer games, based on cartoons, external and other pop culture crossovers.
Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, admits it was a tough year for the series.
"I think we missed expectations with our community last year," he tells BBC Newsbeat.
"So we took a step back, we listened to them."
Players now have the ability to switch off controversial cosmetic changes, and Bahl says Modern Warfare 4 is a "return to form".
It's a message they've been keen to get out.
This year it's launching just weeks before GTA 6 - arguably the most anticipated video game of the decade.
Despite rising console prices, there's hope that the massive interest in Rockstar Games' ultra-blockbuster will convince people to buy a new console or return to the hobby.
Bahl says GTA 6 and Call of Duty are "the two biggest games of the year" but they're not necessarily in direct competition.
"More people dusting off their Xbox or their PlayStation, starting to play for the first time it gives an opportunity for more gamers to come in and play both of the games," says Bahl.
GTA 6 will only be released on PlayStation 5 and Xbox consoles at first, and multiplayer modes won't be available at launch.
"So we feel like this is differentiated enough to really stand out," says Bahl.
The game itself sells for about £70 in the UK, but Bahl points out it can be a year-round hangout space for many fans.
"The number one reason people come to Call of Duty is not just for the combat or the gunplay, but it's actually because their friends are there, right?
"And so that social connection is so powerful."
One of the biggest criticisms of last year's Call of Duty was its single-player campaign mode.
The short, cinematic adventures are rarely the main reason players pick up the latest title, but are nevertheless popular.
Alternating titles in the series follow different storylines, and the Modern Warfare strand has produced some of Call of Duty's most beloved characters.
Activision has said Modern Warfare 4 is the "epic conclusion" to the story of fan favourite Capt John Price, played by British actor Barry Sloane.
"It's a lot of surprises, a culmination of all those pieces that we've been putting together coming together," he says.
Sloane tells Newsbeat he's not too intimidated by the weight of expectation.
"I've been greeted with love from the fan base since the get-go," he says.
María Elisa Camargo, who returns to the series as cartel leader Valeria Garza, admits the fanbase is "a tough crowd".
"They're very smart, very story-driven, and they're not just loving anyone," she says.
Actor Mads Mikkelsen, known for appearances in films such as Casino Royale and TV show Hannibal, plays mysterious enemy The Archer.
He says there's at least one player who'll be there to play through the campaign.
"I know for sure my son will try to kill me again and again.

items.title: Celebrity Traitors - paranoia deepens as traitor behaviour splits opinion
paragraphs: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode seven of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.
Six days is a long time in The Celebrity Traitors.

So it was a relief to be put out of our misery as last Friday's literal yawn-fest came to its slow-burning conclusion; the traitorous trio eventually succeeding in their mission to kill in plain sight.
The snoozefest - which involved reluctant traitor James Acaster making faithful Ross Kemp yawn by boring him to tears - meant the paranoid EastEnders star was finally put out of his misery.
On learning his fate, the actor turned to Shakespeare - who else?
"To thine own self be true," he declared, quoting Polonius from Hamlet.
As usual at breakfast, the faithfuls seated early mused over who may have been murdered overnight: "If Jerry's not here, I don't think I can handle it," Romesh Ranganathan confessed.
Jerry Hall was charmingly late to the party. After everyone had discussed Ross's demise, she piped up in her famous Texan drawl: "Is Ross gone?"

As the typical off-the-wall theories began to swirl, Jerry later told Miranda Hart she suspected fellow faithful James Blunt - for the very plausible reason that "his face is redder than a fox's ass at gooseberry time". It's as good a reason as any proffered so far this series.

Once the croissant crumbs had been cleared, it was time for a mission that threw the cat among the pigeons - not least because the traitor's lair it took place in "smelled like a litter tray", according to Jerry.
Miranda felt there were more complex olfactory notes at play: "A mix of salmon, cheap cologne and crotch." Delightful.
The mission involved each player having to build a shield on a plinth in front of them out of 3D jigsaw-type pieces which were buried in troughs in sawdust. Think Krypton Factor meets lucky dip.

At three intervals, a bell would ring, and the players all had to stop and put on blindfolds for a few minutes. The traitors could then remove theirs and go about sabotaging the handiwork of anyone they fancied.
And while James A revealed he was "starting to have more fun" after murdering poor Ross, if there was a prize for the worst traitor of all time, he would still smash it.

He was too scared to take off his blindfold and remove any shield pieces from the faithfuls, leaving the dirty work - and all the risk - to fellow traitors Maya Jama and King Kenny. Suffice to say, they were not impressed.
"He didn't even lift the blindfold off - I'm speechless," said Maya.
James A knew he was in trouble: "I'm aware I'll get a dressing down in the turret but I am the one who killed Grant Mitchell."
He wasn't wrong about the telling off. And the fact he completed his own puzzle, earning himself a shield, must have really riled his co-conspirators.
To be fair, you could argue he's playing a blinder - there's been very little suspicion of him so far.

Three other celebrities also managed to complete their shield puzzles - James B, Joanne McNall and Michael Sheen - but no money was banked after Maya and Kenny panicked and didn't remove any pieces at their last opportunity.

But the task at least threw up another bunch of mad theories for the faithfuls to chew over, as they tried to unsuccessfully guess where the floorboard creaking was coming from as two of the traitors tried to creep around the room.
It was good news for Romesh at least, whose hay fever saved the day - Sharon Rooney could hear him sniffing constantly next to her so knew he couldn't have been a traitor.
Maybe the tickly moustache isn't helping his allergies - and combing it won't make much difference.
Ahead of the round table, self-styled "Poundland Poirot" Sharon was living up to her nickname with a red herring theory about a perfume bottle being used to kill someone in plain sight.
Ross's murder and the disorienting mission ultimately confused everyone, with the round table being the most random of the series so far.

Leigh-Ann Pinnock, Bash Croft, Joanne and Jerry were among the accused, with Jerry - having survived murder overnight - banished for being "a professional pot stirrer. She's "planted more seeds than a farmer's market" – or at least that was Joanne's reasoning.
Romesh's deadpan excuse was better: "I've long suspected she preferred Rob (his comedy partner and former contestant Rob Beckett) to me."
Once again, the faithfuls were left to rue losing one of their own, with Jerry chastising them as she made her grand exit: "I told you so!"
Leigh-Ann still had heat on her after Jerry's banishment, with her bright red - blood red? - leather-look long gloves drawing attention in the kitchen.
"I said they looked traitorous and villainous," she bemoaned.
Back in the turret, as James A predicted, Maya and Kenny were not happy about his lack of action at the mission.
"You hung us out to dry!" Maya chastised him.
But he redeemed himself somewhat by declaring that he had finally got a taste for villainy.
"When I killed Ross Kemp in plain sight, I loved it!" James A told a delighted Maya and Kenny.
It's only taken him three-quarters of the series to get there but better late than never.
Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday
The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked

items.title: North Korea’s secretive prison camps: building the case for accountability
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

North Korea has continued to expand and renovate detention facilities across the country, while estimates of the number of prisoners held in its political prison camps vary widely, reflecting the limited information available about the secretive system.

Seoul-based state-funded Korea Institute for National Unification estimated in its most recent report, published last year, that between 53,000 and 65,000 people were being held in four operating political prison camps.
South Korea-based news agency Daily NK recently cited an unnamed source inside North Korea as estimating that about 147,000 people were being held across six camps.

Greg Scarlatoiu, president of the Washington-based Committee for Human Rights in North Korea, told VOA he believes the “current political prison camp population could be closer to 200,000.” The figures, however, are not directly comparable because they are based on different sources, methodologies, and assumptions.

North Korea continues to deny that political prison camps exist and has long barred international investigators from accessing its detention facilities. As a result, satellite imagery has become one of the few available tools for monitoring developments inside the country's highly restricted prison system.

According to Daily NK, which employs several north Korean defectors, at least 14 detention facilities have been built or remodeled since late 2023. The sites include re-education prisons as well as other detention facilities. Experts caution, however, that construction activity alone does not prove that the detainee population has increased.

Ethan Hee-seok Shin, a member of the U.N. Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, told VOA that political prisoners in North Korea “can face imprisonment without trial, lifelong forced labor and punishment that extends to family members under the state's system of guilt by association."
Such practices, Shin said, “help create a climate of fear that reaches far beyond the prison camps themselves."

Experts say satellite imagery can reveal new buildings, expanded perimeters and enhanced security infrastructure, but it cannot determine how many people are being detained or identify individual perpetrators of alleged abuses. For that reason, testimony from former detainees and insiders, along with internal government documents, remains essential for documenting alleged human rights violations and establishing responsibility.

Shin called for stronger international efforts to collect, preserve, and analyze evidence that could be used in future accountability processes. Scarlatoiu said those “efforts should be coupled with broader initiatives to increase North Koreans' access to outside information,” arguing that greater awareness of the outside world “remains a critical tool for long-term change."

items.title: Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix
paragraphs: Lewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain racing in Formula One until he can take part in the African Grand Prix which is set to take place in Rwanda in the 2030s, with the seven-time world champion also stating he believes it is right that F1 is to hold a race there despite criticism of the country’s human rights record.

Last week F1 confirmed Rwanda was to host the African Grand Prix having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It is lined up to be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital, Kigali, which has yet to be constructed and marks a return to the African continent for the first time since it last held a race at Kyalami, South Africa in 1993.

Hamilton has been championing a race in Africa for some time. The 41-year-old is understood to be currently contracted with Ferrari until the end of the 2027 season, and speaking before this weekend’s US Grand Prix he said he would like to continue racing for at least another four years in order to make it to the meeting in Rwanda.

“I’m now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that’s been my dream to be able to race in Africa,” he said. “So, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we’ll keep it going.”
Hamilton would be at least in his mid-40s if he was to continue until 2030. F1’s current oldest driver is 45-year-old Fernando Alonso.
F1’s deal with Rwanda is for a 10-year period but because of the country’s human rights record the award of the race has been criticised as an act of sportswashing.

“A 10-year grand prix ‘presented by Visit Rwanda’ is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities,” said Felix Jakens, Amnesty UK’s head of campaigns. “Rwanda is buying into the world’s biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from ⁠its appalling human rights record. Formula One says sport can be ‘a positive force for good’. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Rwanda’s authorities are prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech.”
Hamilton nonetheless felt the meeting would serve as a force for good in Africa and that there also should be more education about the continent.

“I’m really, really hopeful for that grand prix,” he said. “Of course, I don’t get to choose where we go, and naturally there’s problems all over the world today, so I’ve seen many of the stories but I think we really have to approach it with humility.”

“There’s a lot that we don’t know. I mean, growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism, and the West intervening.

“I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there’s many people that don’t want that to happen, because they would be so powerful if they did, but I’m still hopeful that at some stage they will.”

The new race is being backed by the government of Rwanda and the Rwanda Development Board, who intend to develop the venue as a destination not only for motorsport but for promoting economic growth. The country has recently invested heavily in hosting sporting events, including cycling’s road world championships, cricket’s Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 Fifa congress and the Basketball Africa League.
Hamilton felt that at least the race would present an opportunity for people to take a greater interest in Africa.

“Going doesn’t mean that you neglect the things that are happening there,” he said. “Hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more of what is happening there, what has happened there for hundreds of years and I hope that does spark the conversation. Then I guess I’ll finish it off with, I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping that at some stage we get to.”

Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli goes into this weekend US Grand Prix in a position to clinch his first F1 title. The 20-year-old holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Hamilton is fifth or lower.

items.title: Burnham to reveal plans for AI unit to tackle wildfires after scorching summer
paragraphs: The UK government is to create an AI Cobra unit to spot wildfires after this year’s record-breaking summer saw devastating blazes across the country.

The country experienced its hottest-ever summer this year, with prolonged dry periods and extreme heat fuelling wildfires that triggered an emergency alert to mobile phones in England and Wales. Figures released on 8 October showed a clear upward trend in the number of fires recorded each year.
The Met Office found that the climate crisis made this extreme heat about 130 times more likely.

At the government’s first wildfire resilience summit on Friday, Andy Burnham will announce plans for a new wildfire AI unit in the National Situation Centre, which is part of the Cobra briefing rooms.

Businesses including Google, Airbus and VodafoneThree are expected to attend the summit to set out how satellite monitoring and early warning systems can help fight fires. The government said its new AI unit would enable it to “spot and fight fires faster”.
The prime minister will also announce £45m for fire crews to buy wildfire-specific personal protective equipment (PPE).
This comes after the Guardian revealed that more than half of the 29 fire services that responded to requests for information had no wildfire PPE.

They included the Suffolk fire and rescue service, which had to deal with an “apocalyptic” wildfire earlier this summer that burned close to the Sizewell B nuclear power station and destroyed vast areas of a protected nature reserve.
Standard particle-filtering respirators do not protect against dangerous gases such as carbon monoxide, which are heavily present in wildfire smoke.
Standard PPE can also be too hot and heavy for wildfire conditions. This can cause crews to overheat, or remove their PPE altogether, exposing them to greater danger from heat, smoke and radiation.
The prime minister will also announce that military planes and helicopters will be made available to fight wildfires on remote moorland, steep hillsides and other hard-to-reach terrain.

The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said: “As the threat of wildfires in the UK grows, defence will step up to provide greater support to our emergency services and protect military training areas across the country.”

The government will also look at tougher local restrictions or product bans to stop people starting fires when the risk is high. In August, Burnham announced a temporary ban on sales of disposable barbecues. He has also been criticised for failing to address the climate emergency in his wildfire response.

Farmers will also be given funding to make landscapes more resilient to fires. This announcement comes after the government quietly scrapped plans announced under the Conservative government to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires.

This revelation led Alistair Carmichael, a Scottish Liberal Democrat MP and chair of the Commons environment, food and rural affairs committee, to raise “serious questions about whether this summer’s wildfires could have looked different with more resources on the ground”.

The government also said it would allocate £25m to restore dried-out peatlands in England so they hold more water and act as natural firebreaks, as well as provide financial support for farmers to fireproof their land.
This new grant scheme is expected to run from April 2027 to April 2029.

Environmental campaigner and author Guy Shrubsole said: “For decades, wealthy grouse moor owners have drained our peat bogs, turning them into a tinderbox. This grant will help reverse that destruction, but must be followed by a new round of landscape recovery funding, and duties on landowners to repair the damage done. It’s time to make England wet again.”

The prime minister said: “I stood in Stourbridge and watched families lose everything. I will never forget it. Our firefighters were heroes that day, but heroes shouldn’t have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs.
“Crews will now have the kit they need to stay safe and military aircraft will stand ready to help tackle wildfires from the sky. We cannot put people through another summer like this one.”

items.title: Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton Show
paragraphs: The Prince of Wales has made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize.
During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize.
As Norton spoke about the initiative with the trio he surprised the audience by then inviting the prince out to join them on the sofa.
They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. The prize was founded by William to "celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet".
The guests also chatted about William's long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films.
William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, drawing inspiration from US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.
There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives £1m.
The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year's winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November.

Last year, the ceremony for the prizes drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro.
The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for "transforming one of the world's most wasteful industries" by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability.
At last year's ceremony, William said the winners were "proof that progress is possible".
The Graham Norton Show is on BBC One at 22.40 Friday.

items.title: US actor Tom Skerritt, star of Top Gun, Steel Magnolias and Alien, dies aged 93
paragraphs: US actor Tom Skerritt, who starred in the TV series Picket Fences and the films Alien and Top Gun, has died aged 93, his family says.

Skerritt died on Wednesday of natural causes, his family said, adding: "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humour, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives."
In a six-decade career, he appeared in the film Mash, A River Runs Through It and Ted. He also co-founded TheFilmSchool in Seattle to support next-generation filmmakers and storytellers.
His family said he will be remembered "for his belief that stories can help people heal, find purpose and create change".
The moustachioed star of several 20th Century hit films was born in 1933 in Detroit, Michigan, and served in the US Air Force before pursuing an acting career that boasted several military roles.
He made his film debut in 1962 alongside a young Robert Redford ​in War Hunt and years later reunited with Redford in the 1992 period drama A River Runs Through It, which starred Brad Pitt.
Skerritt's breakthrough role came when he played US army surgeon Duke Forrest in the 1970 Korean War comedy Mash, which also starred Donald Sutherland, Elliott Gould and Sally Kellerman.
The hit film, which was released amid unrest over the Vietnam War, was nominated for five Academy Awards and was adapted for television two years later.
He also starred alongside Sigourney Weaver in the 1979 sci-fi film Alien, which earned two Oscar nominations, and led to three sequels and several crossover projects.
"It is spontaneity and impulse ​that make the difference, and that is ⁠what I felt we had with 'Alien'," Skerritt said in a 2019 interview, according to news agency Reuters.
"Every one of us had that immediate rapport with each other."
Skerritt said that one of the things he liked most when he first read the script was that "the woman becomes a hero", referring to Weaver's character, Ripley.
During his career, he starred opposite several strong female leads.
He appeared with Shirley MacLaine in the 1977 film Turning Point and played Sally Field's husband in 1989's Steel Magnolias.
As Cdr Mike "Viper" Metcalf in the 1986 classic Top Gun, the versatile actor appeared alongside a young Tom Cruise.
On television, he won an Emmy Award in 1993 for his role as Sheriff Jimmy Brock in David E Kelley's drama Picket Fences.
The quirky procedural's ensemble cast was nominated for Sag Awards in 1995 and 1996 and he received a nod for male actor in a drama series in 1995.
Lauren Holly, who played Skerritt's deputy on Picket Fences, described him in a tribute as "our leader".
"His example made those years such a joy and we all loved and respected him so much," Holly wrote.

"He cared deeply for his family - both the one at home and the one at work. He cared deeply for his planet and all of its inhabitants. He had a huge impact on my life and so many memories I have of him include sharing fits of crippling laughter."

Skerritt also had guest roles on the small screen in The West Wing, Madam Secretary, Law & Order: SVU and Huff. He reteamed with Field as the family patriarch, William Walker, in the drama Brothers & Sisters from 2007-09.

items.title: Iran-based news site says Supreme Court upholds death sentence for political prisoner months after granting him reprieve
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

An Iranian news site says the regime’s Supreme Court has upheld a death sentence on a political prisoner months after granting a reprieve to the man, convicted of causing minor damage to a judiciary building.

In a Wednesday Telegram post, the Emtedad outlet run by the Union of Islamic Iran People Party said the Supreme Court upheld “in the past week” a death sentence issued by Branch 1 of the Rasht Revolutionary Court against Manouchehr Fallah several months ago. Rasht is the capital of northern Iran’s Gilan province.

The Rasht Revolutionary Court’s Branch 2 previously handed Fallah a death sentence in the same case in early 2025 and the Supreme Court upheld it. But the top court overturned that decision early this year on appeal from Fallah’s lawyer and ordered a retrial.

Fallah, who is around 42 years old, has been detained in Rasht’s Lakan Prison. Emtedad said he is enduring “very heavy psychological pressure” from having his death sentence overturned and then re-imposed.

Emtedad said Branch 2 initially sentenced Fallah to death on the charge of “destruction with the intent of confronting the Islamic government” for causing 15 million tomans in damage to the door of the Rasht judiciary building. The damage was worth about $180 at the open-market rate at the time of the sentencing.

Defense lawyer Milad Panahipour wrote on Emtedad last October that Fallah, his client, was accused of detonating a small firecracker in front of the judicial office’s entrance at 12:30am on June 1, 2023. Panahipour said the detonation caused minor damage to the building’s iron door and stone facade and hurt no one.

Emtedad said Panahipour petitioned the Supreme Court for a retrial and cited the lawyer as saying that request was granted earlier this year. The outlet said Fallah’s case was referred to Branch 1, a parallel court, for the retrial, and rights groups reported that the judge issued a new death sentence against the political prisoner in May.
The Emtedad report said Fallah’s re-confirmed death sentence has been referred to the Rasht Criminal Sentence Execution Unit for implementation.
Exiled Iranian human rights groups HRANA and Hengaw have said Fallah was denied access to legal representation during his initial proceedings and was tried by video link in December 2024.

The United States has repeatedly condemned the Islamic republic's use of the death penalty to suppress political dissent. The State Department also has emphasized the necessity of respecting defendants' rights, including access to legal representation and a fair trial.

The Treasury Department sanctioned several Iranian officials in January 2026 for their roles in suppressing protesters. In that announcement, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his department “will use every tool to target those behind the regime's tyrannical oppression of human rights.”

items.title: Autex Acoustics panels "place sound at the heart" of Manchester's Bar Shrimp
paragraphs: Acoustic brand Autex Acoustics has equipped Manchester’s Bar Shrimp with sound-enhancing acoustic panels, creating an “immersive and energetic space” dedicated to music listening.
Bar Shrimp is a seafood-serving music destination designed to provide a high-quality music experience within a relaxed environment.

The bar’s interior combines luxury acoustic panels, layered textures, rich red tones, and atmospheric lighting to create an intimate space that can switch from a relaxed dining setting to a vibrant late-night venue.

The bar’s walls were furnished with Autex Acoustics’ Mirage finish, a lightweight acoustic panel made from PET, customised using a precision laser etching technique to create a distinctive textured aesthetic.
The finish softens reverberation from the bar’s concrete floors, while its textured, soft appearance adds to the venue’s relaxed visual identity.

According to Autex Acoustics, Mirage also controls background chatter and balances music played throughout the space, which, according to Bar Shimp’s co-founder Richard Cossins, was one of the key parts of the bar’s design.

“Our mission at Bar Shrimp is to place sound at the heart of the venue, treating it as an integral part of the experience,” said Cossins. “The goal is to deliver an immersive sonic identity, detailed and balanced within the space.”
Above the bar, an Autex Acoustics’ Frontier Axis system was also added for its striking grid-like appearance and additional sound-absorbing qualities.
Autex Acoustics products are made in the UK from at least 80 per cent recycled content.
According to Cossins, the project was built on a shared understanding of how sound and acoustics can shape people’s experience of a venue, whilst also aligning on sustainability values.
“In hospitality, sound panelling is often an afterthought,” said director at Autex Acoustics UK and EU, Daniel Senior.
“But what we’ve learned with the team at Bar Shrimp is that acoustics can actually elevate the design and be an integral part of it.”
Bar Shrimp was named “Manchester’s new best thing ever” by Guardian food critic Grace Dent, and it is the third collaboration between Cossins and Autex Acoustics.
Autex Acoustics crafts acoustic products that combine decades of expertise with innovative solutions that aim to enhance both the visual and acoustic experience of interior spaces.
The brand has recently launched Raft, the latest addition to the Frontier range, which combines sculptural acoustic design with “significantly reduced embodied carbon and material use”.
To learn more about Autex Acoustics, visit its website.

items.title: Facade of Mexican university building draws on Gothic architecture
paragraphs: Mexican studio Jonathan Corral Arquitectos has completed an educational building called the UAD Alamedas Tower, which features a faceted facade that takes cues from stained-glass windows found in Gothic cathedrals.
The building is part of the Universidad Durango Santander, or UAD, a private institution with campuses in several Mexican states.
For its Durango location, the university acquired a site overlooking Las Alamedas, a prominent, tree-lined promenade that stretches through the heart of the city.
Responding to this context was a key concern for the building’s designer, local studio Jonathan Corral Arquitectos.

“The project establishes its relationship with this setting through an intermediate condition – an architecture with a clear urban presence, whose scale and materiality engage with the existing landscape,” said the team.
Triangular in plan, the 7,987-square-metre building contains eight levels and a basement.

A variety of spaces are found in the building, including classrooms, studios, meeting rooms, auditoriums, offices, a cafeteria and a courtroom for mock trials, among other spaces. The school offers courses in law, architecture, medicine, sciences, communication technologies and gastronomy.
On the exterior, the building appears as multiple structures given the use of varying facade treatments.
Along the main elevation, which faces north, one portion is clad in grey fibre-cement panels, while another is lined with a black metal screen.
The central portion features a glazed elevator and a faceted curtain wall with dark mullions and triangular panes of glass – a design that draws upon Gothic architecture.
“The large glazed surface of the facade draws on the compositional logic of the Gothic stained-glass window, translating it into a contemporary urban scale,” the team said.
While the front elevation is meant to be transparent, the rear wall is more opaque. It has grey cladding and short, horizontal windows.
The main entrance is fronted by a broad stone staircase that doubles as a plaza. The building is elevated above grade to help protect from potential flooding, the team said.
Visitors enter a full-height atrium, ringed by walkways with frosted glass railings. The atrium is meant to establish “visual continuity” between the interior spaces and the adjacent promenade.
“From within, the urban landscape is framed by different levels and circulation routes, keeping the context a constant presence throughout the building experience,” the team said.
The lobby features a sunken plaza wrapped in black marble and a suspended staircase, which acts as a sculptural element.
The building’s structural elements were left exposed in many areas.
The building’s basement – which contains digital research and consultation space – has exposed concrete walls and flooring.
On the top level – which holds three auditoriums – a pine-lattice ceiling is meant to be “in dialogue with exposed structures and ducts, as well as steel railings”.
“Rather than concealing the logic of construction, the solution allows structure and program to share a common architectural expression,” the team said.
The building is topped with a rooftop terrace, where people can gather and take in views of the city.

Other university projects in Mexico include a business school by a team of architects in the city of Aguascalientes, which features courtyards and lush gardens, and a Tatiana Bilbao-designed biotechnology building in Mexico City that is composed of irregularly stacked glass boxes.
Design architect: Jonathan Corral Contreras Design team: Heriberto Díaz Ortega, Aida Uribe, Sergio Cisneros, Osvaldo Medina, Julio Rodriguez
Contractor: Forum Constructura, Martin Soriano Villanueva, Fernando Soriano Villanueva
Structural engineering: Jesús González Flores
Photography by Recording Architecture (unless stated otherwise)

items.title: US rejects China’s claim of ‘unauthorized trespassing’ after warship sails through disputed reef
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.
The U.S. has rejected China's claim that a U.S. warship trespassed its territorial waters and urged Beijing to halt its "aggressive" maneuvers in the South China Sea.

China on Tuesday dispatched naval forces to monitor the transit of the USS Charleston near the disputed Sabina Shoal in the South China Sea.A spokesperson for China's military on Tuesday accused the U.S. of “infringing upon China’s sovereignty rights and interests.”
Chinese official media outlets described the littoral combat ship’s passage as an “unauthorized trespassing.”
The U.S. rejects China's claim and asserted that Beijing's attempted enforcement of its “unlawful maritime claims” undermines regional stability.
Washington has also accused Beijing of asserting what it terms as "unlawful maritime claims in most of the South China Sea.”

“The United States will fly, sail, and operate wherever international law allows, including the South China Sea," a spokesperson for the State Department said in response to VOA inquiry about the China's criticism of the passage of USS Charleston.
“Freedom of the seas and adherence to the international law of the sea is vital for the entire international community,” the spokesperson added.

But does China have the right to require U.S. warships to provide prior notification—or even obtain approval—before passing through the Sabina Shoal? Regardless of the sovereignty claims, how does the physical and geographical location of Sabina Shoal relate to this dispute?
Does Sabina Shoal have territorial rights under international law?
Sabina Shoal, a coral atoll in the contested Spratly Islands, is located approximately 75 nautical miles west of the Philippine island of Palawan.

The Philippines, which refers to it as Escoda Shoal, considers it to be within its 200-nautical-mile Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). China, which claims almost all of the vast South China Sea as its territory, refers to the shoal as Xianbin Reef.
A key point of contention concerns how Sabina Shoal is classified as a natural feature and the maritime rights it may—or may not—generate under international maritime law.
Peter Dutton, a senior research scholar in law and senior fellow in the Paul Tsai China Center at Yale Law School, argues that the shoal has no territorial sea or other entitlements.
He says that Sabina Shoal is a "low-tide elevation," which has specific legal connotations under Article 13 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).

"It is a low tide elevation, meaning there is no part of the shoal that is permanently above water," he told VOA. “The law considers low tide elevations to be part of the continental shelf of the nearest coastal state. In this case, that is the Philippines."
The waters surrounding the shoal are in an area of high seas freedoms unless the territorial sea of another nearby feature encompasses the shoal, Dutton argues.
"But even in that case, warships such as the USS Charleston are legally entitled to undertake ‘innocent passage’ around the shoal," he said.
Does China have the right to demand prior notification from U.S. warships?

China’s 1992 Law on the Territorial Sea and the Contiguous Zone requires foreign military vessels to obtain approval from the Chinese government before entering China’s territorial sea, a position disputed by experts.

Lowell Bautista, an Associate Professor at Western Sydney University School of Law in Australia, believes that China cannot, based solely on its own sovereignty claims, mandate that foreign warships obtain permission or provide advance notification before navigating through these waters.

Citing Articles 58 and 87 of the UNCLOS, Bautista says vessels of all states—including warships—enjoy freedom of navigation within an EEZ and generally do not require prior authorization from the coastal state.

"China argues that foreign military activities in an EEZ require its consent, but that view is not supported by the convention and is rejected by most maritime states," he told VOA. "In any case, a transit is an exercise of navigation, the most basic freedom the convention protects."

Bautista says that although the U.S. is not a party to UNCLOS, it accepts and adheres to many of the convention’s rules regarding freedom of navigation as a matter of customary international law. China, by contrast, is a party to the convention and is bound by its provisions, he said.
The U.S. has urged China to "cease its dangerous and aggressive behavior."

The State Department spokesperson also called on China to comply with its treaty obligations to comport its maritime claims in the South China Sea to the requirements of the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and the 2016 Arbitral Tribunal ruling.

“China’s attempted enforcement of its unlawful maritime claims undermines regional stability, as well as the legal rights and freedoms of the United States and all other countries and claimants," the spokesperson said, highlighting the importance of the freedom of the seas and adherence to the international law.
In July 2016, an international arbitral tribunal in The Hague ruled that there is no legal basis for China’s expansive maritime claims in the South China Sea.
The U.S., the Philippines and 12 other nations issued a joint statement last July reaffirming that The Hague ruling is “final” and “legally binding.”

items.title: Meta shields Mark Zuckerberg from possible 'billionaires tax' hit
paragraphs: Meta has agreed a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to stop the Facebook co-founder from leaving California after he threatened to move from the state because of a proposed tax on billionaires.
The agreement allows Zuckerberg - reportedly one of the world's richest people - to sell shares in Meta without losing control of the Californian-based company if he needs to pay a large tax bill.
The measure, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on state residents with a net worth of more than $1bn (£750m), is yet to pass. Californian residents will vote on 3 November.
Nevertheless, Zuckerberg secured a deal with a special committee at Meta after "robust", and "at several points, contentious" negotiations.
California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.
Zuckerberg - who has a $226bn fortune according to Forbes' billionaires tracker - had told Meta's board that it was his intention to remain with the firm for "the foreseeable future".

However, he said he was evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California and, if he listed his home on the real estate market, it "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees".
This, he told the board, "would raise questions for management of the company going forward".

A special committee within Meta decided it was "critically important" to keep Zuckerberg in a leadership role and in California to manage the firm from its headquarters "during this era of unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry".
Tech companies in the US and globally are spending billions of dollars on developing artificial intelligence and the infrastructure around it.
Meta said the share deal was appropriate to ensure Zuckerberg "remains working closely" with the company's AI at its headquarters.
It said his "talent and leadership have been crucial to our growth, strategy, and stability since our inception, and the special committee wants that to continue".

items.title: There's suddenly $1,000 off this absolute beast of a creative laptop cut out for heavy video editing and 3D rendering
paragraphs: The RAM crisis has caused laptop prices to soar this year, which has been terrible for creatives and gamers alike. The good news is that you might not have to wait to Black Friday to find the best prices since the hikes came into effect. B&H has $400 of the 15in Lenovo Legion 5a and $1,000 off the 16in Lenovo Legion Pro i7.

With dedicated Nvidia graphics cards, both of these laptops cater to creators as much as gamers. The 5a has you covered for photo editing, 2D design work and content creation, while the Legion Pro i7 has the internals for heavier video editing and 3D rendering workflows as well as AAA gaming with RTX 5080 graphics and 32GB RAM.

There are another couple of deals I'd recommend considering if you don't need quite as much power or if you're looking for a lighter device for travel. See below for the details. For more options, see our guides to the best laptops for video editing based on our own reviews. For cheaper laptops, see our guide to the best budget laptops for graphic design students.
Subscribe to the Creative Bloq newsletter for details of expert-curated offers, bringing the tools you need to create – and products perfect for the design-obsessed.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: WHO reports six more polio cases in Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.
The World Health Organization has reported six new poliovirus cases in Afghanistan this week.
In a statement, the WHO said that the six cases of wild poliovirus type 1, or WPV1, were reported in the provinces of Kandahar, Nangarhar, and Kabul.
The WHO said so far this year, 48 positive cases of the wild poliovirus have been registered globally, 42 of which are in Afghanistan and six in Pakistan.
The number represents a sharp increase from last year.
In 2025, 52 positive wild poliovirus cases were reported worldwide, including 21 in Afghanistan and 31 in Pakistan.
Before the Taliban imposed a ban on house-to-house polio vaccination in Afghanistan, the number of positive poliovirus cases was low. There were only two reported cases in 2022 and six in 2023.
However, the Taliban, in September 2024, banned house-to-house vaccination campaigns, and the only through site-to-site, including vaccination at mosque and other designated locations.
Polio is an infectious viral disease that largely affects children under 5 years of age.
WPV1 is one of three original strains of wild poliovirus that attacks the nervous system and can cause irreversible paralysis or death.
Pakistan and Afghanistan are the two remaining countries where cases of wild poliovirus type 1 are still reported.
The wild poliovirus types 2 and 3 have been declared eradicated in 2015 and 2019.
New cases are being reported in Afghanistan as the world prepares to mark World Polio Day on Saturday, Oct. 24.
The day is celebrated to raise awareness of the importance of polio vaccination and honor the work of volunteers, health professionals and parents toward eradicating the disease.
Kamal Shah, a former UNICEF communications officer, told VOA that Afghanistan's polio eradication program faces serious challenges as cases rise.
“One of the main issues in implementing the polio eradication campaign is shortcomings in vaccination campaigns,” he said.
Shah added that the lack of public awareness about the virus and other factors, such as malnutrition in children, are compounding the country’s polio problem.

items.title: Tuesday Labs debuts "droid butler" Voxel
paragraphs: New York technology company Tuesday Labs has debuted its first semi-autonomous robot Voxel Series-1, designed to help with household chores and to avoid the appearance of an “uncanny valley” humanoid robot.
Voxel Series-1 (Voxel) performs tasks such as watering plants and sweeping crumbs, which it currently achieves with a combination of autonomous intelligence and teleoperation.

The robot is counter-height and covered in a colourful matte plastic shell with primarily “cuboid” body parts, LED eyes and 1-DOF grippers for hands. Tuesday Labs founder Rosalind Shinkle told Dezeen that initial designs were informed by home objects such as lamps, chairs and briefcases.
Working with former Pixar character designer Alonso Martinez, Shinkle said the finalised Voxel is a combination of “exceptional capability and charming character”.
“We deliberately didn’t build a humanoid,” Shinkle said. “We wanted to stay far from the uncanny valley, and far from robots that fill a human-shaped space in the home.”
“Instead, we made Voxel relatively small and cuboid, to signal his role in your life: a droid butler, not a human butler.”

“We know we don’t want him to feel almost-human, and we know we don’t want him to feel like a toaster,” she continued. “A believable character needs every element sitting at roughly the same point on that human–toaster spectrum.”
Shinkle said five key principles drove the design of Voxel, including easy integration into the home, a maximalist appearance, simplicity, luxury and playfulness.
Part of the strategy was also “affordance matching”, or that, when Voxel is perceived by a human, its capabilities can be inherently understood.

“When someone looks at a robot, they should be able to roughly predict what he’s capable of,” Shinkle said. “If you correctly match perceived and actual affordance, you can avoid that constant feeling of disappointment when a humanoid robot isn’t quite as good at doing things as a human.”
Voxel’s plastic shell and finishes are meant to keep it relatively lightweight, but Shinkle said the external design should also communicate its quality.

Like another home robot that is currently in production, Neo by 1X Technologies, Voxel’s initial customers are “early adopters” who opt in to help informally train the robot’s autonomous software at home.
“We’re starting with a limited number of robots for early adopters who are excited to experience and help shape this technology,” she said.

“Voxel’s estimated price is $20,000, so he will be a luxury product. But our ambition is much bigger – as the technology improves and production scales, we want to make household robots accessible to far more people.”
Shinkle said her own distaste for household chores was part of what drove Voxel.
“Robots will soon be a part of our homes,” she said. “I set out to build the robot that I would actually want to live with.”
“Also, I hate cleaning my apartment, and I’d much rather spend my time building something that solves that problem once and for all.”
Voxel is powered by a rechargeable battery and will charge in an at-home docking station as part of “his normal routine”.

Tuesday Labs is based in New York City and was founded in 2025 by Shinkle, who previously worked as an engineer at Boston Dynamics. The studio is focused on creating “robots that feel natural and delightful to live with”.
The combination of advanced technology and autonomous intelligence has made the creation of robots more possible than ever at this point in history.

This has allowed the field to diversify, and technology companies and studios have released a varity of different types of robots in recent years, including all the cute robots from CES 2025 and five that were displayed at Carlo Ratti’s architecture biennale.
Other recent home robots that debuted include Neo by 1X Technologies and CLOiD by LG.

items.title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
paragraphs: A US judge has ordered President Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.
Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.
Charles Tobin, a lawyer representing the BBC, said in court that "we still haven't been able to depose the plaintiff" with two months left in the discovery period.
Trump cancelled a previous deposition on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance" while he was campaigning in Georgia.
In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings.
The judge in the case, US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett, said that Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December, unless the discovery period is extended.
Last week, attorneys asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place.
On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his property in Mar-a-Lago in Florida.

In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year, and claimed that the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action."
Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.
The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that President Trump made a direct call for violent action".
The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

In July, Trump's lawyers conceded that they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC select or through US broadcasters.
Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, its commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary.
Typically, depositions take place in a lawyer's office - rather than a courtroom - without a judge physically present.
Depositions, however, carry legal weight and take place under oath. They are recorded verbatim by a court reporter, and the transcripts can later be used as evidence during trials.

items.title: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
paragraphs: Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.

Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.
Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.
There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.
Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out.
"The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.
She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".
The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.

A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue".
"But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.
Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented".
"It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One.
But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers.
He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected, external had been received and was being acted on.
Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date.
"Hacking has been around for many years," he said.
"The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point."
Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online.
He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long.
"MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said.
He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers.
PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.
It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit.
When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.
It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today.

PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.
According to cyber-security firm Wiz, external, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites.
And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it.

The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP.
Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems.

Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X, external on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced.
"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added.
Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal.
While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday.
The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday.
But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required.
In France, telecommunications company Orange also said, external it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.

According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally.
"The window to respond has shrunk dramatically," said Matt Hull, VP of cyber intelligence and response at global cyber security company NCC Group.
"A few years ago, attackers might have taken weeks to exploit a vulnerability. Now, it can be days or hours."
Hull also highlighted the extent of the task facing developers and engineers working to deal with the issue.

"Several days into this incident, security professionals might already be dealing with significant burnout," he said, urging a need to "make time to rest, share the workload and look after each other".
"Resilience depends on people as much as technology."

items.title: Prime Minister swaps dispatch box for Gogglebox
paragraphs: Appearing on the edition with the prime minister will be comedian Joe Lycett and Sugababes singers Mutya Buena, Keisha Buchanan and Siobhan Donaghy.
A Channel 4 spokesperson said nothing would be "off limits as Gogglebox continues to celebrate the simple joy of watching television together".
"They'll be sharing hilarious, honest and often unexpected reactions to the week's biggest television moments as well as poignant stories all in aid of Stand Up To Cancer," they added.
Burnham and Rotheram have been friends for many years, serving together as Labour MPs before they both left Parliament to become regional mayors in 2017.

They remained close allies, writing a book together on their vision for Britain's future, and Rotheram was a visible supporter of Burnham's successful campaign to become the MP for Makerfield in June.
The Liverpool City Region mayor said while filming their contributions, he and Burnham had struggled with one particularly cerebral TV quiz show and found themselves flummoxed by its music round.
"We're both big into our music but we couldn't get it," he said.
He added that while their television tastes were largely similar, he and the prime minister disagreed over what snacks to eat while watching.
"I'm more of a cheesy puffs-type guy, but he's more into the hard, crunchy stuff," he said.

items.title: Russell Brand accuser said alleged rape 'really hurt', court hears
paragraphs: Warning - this report contains graphic content
The friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand told a jury the complainant had told her after the alleged attack that it had "really, really hurt".

The witness who spoke via video link at his trial said she had attended the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London with the alleged victim in 2009, where they had been invited to the defendant's dressing room after his comedy show.
Statements from the woman's parents were also heard in court, saying their daughter had told them about the alleged attack, and that she had been "very worried about HIV".
Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.
The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.

The witness said the woman had told her she had visited Brand's house in London soon after meeting at the theatre, and that he then sent a car to collect the woman, which took her to his place in Hampstead.
She said when they spoke about it "quite soon after", she said she "was just crying - really upset".
The witness said Brand had forced her into having anal sex at the end of an encounter that started off consensually.
"He was quite aggressive," she said her friend had told her.
"He forcibly put it in my bum and "it really really hurt".
The witness says she remembers specifically asking the complainant if she had said no to Brand when the alleged attack started.
She said the woman replied "lots of times".
"She told me that she was in a lot of pain" and that "she couldn't sit down".
Another friend of the same complainant also gave evidence to the court.
From the witness box, she told the jury her friend had told her that she had told him to stop during the alleged rape.
She said her friend had said the worst moment had been after the act, and "she said that Brand told her she'd been dirty and had to clean up her mess".
"She said he was quite cold and keen to get her gone".
The witness said she had given her friend advice after she had confided in her.
"I told her that she should go and get checked out because she had anal tears and a lot of discomfort and to seek guidance from her parents and to go to the police.
"She just wasn't sure - it was all a bit chaotic in her head. She felt like it wasn't worth it."
She told jurors: "She didn't think she would be believed, and she didn't think it would be worth it to go.
Statements from the alleged rape victim's parents said their daughter stayed with them for about two months after the alleged incident with Brand.
Her mother's statement said: "I just remember her saying 'he raped me'.
"She was very worried about HIV," she said, adding that her daughter had started talking about it during a car journey.
"She said she went to his place, went to see him, as she had always admired him."
Her father recalled their daughter being "very upset and very unwell", during the stay, that that she was "upset by something that had happened to her."
The father said in his statement that his daughter told him: "They were having sex, she asked him to stop, she kept saying she had been assaulted.
"I turned to her in the car and asked if she asked him to stop, and she said 'no' several times.
"I said 'you have been raped, that's rape'."
He said his daughter got a sexual health check, and he said he had only recently learned his daughter is accusing Brand of anal rape.

items.title: ‘The tech bro fight club is real!’ The titans of AI get the Succession treatment in a wild new TV show
paragraphs: Showrunner Jonathan Glatzer wanted the tagline of his latest TV creation to be: “We’re so fucked.” He laughs. “Sadly it got rejected by the network. Hey, maybe I can use it for season two!” The show in question is The Audacity, his darkly comic drama about AI tech titans. Instead, it went with the more PG tagline “Move fast and break people” – a twist on “Move fast and break things”, the Facebook motto coined by Mark Zuckerberg. The Audacity promises to do for tech bros what Succession did for legacy media. Considering Glatzer is a former writer on Succession, that is no empty threat.

This acerbic and all-too-timely Silicon Valley satire follows CEO Duncan Park (played by Billy Magnussen), the obscenely wealthy founder of a data analytics company. He’s a self-proclaimed “inventor of the future” who also happens to be a morally bankrupt man-baby. “Duncan is worth about half a billion,” says Glatzer. “Naturally, that’s not enough. He desperately wants to be a billionaire and ascend to what we call ‘God Mountain’. But he’s no God.”

Like Succession, The Audacity’s scripts are liberally spiced with baroque swearing. Park boasts about keeping investors “moist” and “Viagra-ing the share price to keep it up”. Magnussen delivers such juicy dialogue with relish. “Jonathan has a way of painting a picture with words while also getting nasty with it,” he grins. “My favourite line in season two is: ‘I pulled it out of my ass and it came out clean.’ You’ll have to wait and see what it refers to.” It’s a measure of The Audacity’s whip-smart relevance that the second season was commissioned before the first had even aired.

“Unquestionably, there’s a tech bro mentality that is sexualised,” says Glatzer. “Silicon Valley is such a male-dominated culture. It’s also very white or south Asian. When I first came here, I didn’t see a person of colour for two weeks. That struck me as very odd in a major US city. Hiring practices are dictated by algorithms. The algorithms say that if you went to these universities, you’re our man. If you came from someplace else, and are maybe not a man, the algorithm says you might be problematic. And you could end up writing a book about us.”

The Audacity pulls no punches on how the tech sector is wrecking the planet. “It sure is,” says Glatzer. “Generative AI is environmentally ruinous. Datacentres are tremendous suckers of energy. Worryingly, it doesn’t take too many rampantly ambitious entrepreneurs to fuck up an entire planet for the rest of us.” When Park is warned about the huge carbon footprint of his “algo”, he shrugs: “I’ll sponsor a penguin.”

Zach Galifianakis plays billionaire genius Carl Bardolph, who “basically created spam”. He’s rich enough to retire but becomes a disruptor out of boredom. “I’ve always been very concerned about the people running tech,” says Galifianakis. “They have math minds, but that sometimes comes with a lack of empathy. About 12 nerds are controlling our lives and designing our futures. And they all tend to have the same profile. Most come from Stanford University. I don’t know what they’re teaching there.” He laughs. “It’s weird and kind of evil.”

Did Galifianakis base his portrayal on anyone specific? “He’s pulled from one dude I’ve watched over the years. I won’t give his name but he’s a real piece of shit. A major jerk. The guys running Silicon Valley are damaged. Carl has a giant hole in his heart and a ton of anger because of his dad. I’ve seen a lot of men like that in Hollywood, so I drew on them too. Most of the puppet masters are egomaniac weirdos and I wouldn’t mind saying that to their faces. Zuckerberg has something missing. Elon Musk is bizarre. They’re little boys. You almost feel sorry for them.”

“Duncan also deals with daddy issues and a lack of love,” says Magnussen. “A lot of tech bros are trying to fill voids. The great irony is that the most antisocial people work in social media. Those who don’t know how to be personable are controlling how we communicate. It’s nuts.”

Both actors view the show as a howl of protest. “I’ve done some cool shit in my career,” says Magnussen. “I’ve been in Bond [he played a CIA agent in No Time to Die]. I’ve been in fun, escapist movies. But this feels different. It’s a call to arms. People need to wake up to the audacious behaviour of this handful of people. Their decisions affect 8.3 billion people. That’s scary, man. I just hope our show opens some conversations. We’ve got to start making a difference.”

Galifianakis agrees. “It’s a warning. I’ve never felt this way before with my work – come on, I was in a movie with a baby wearing sunglasses [The Hangover] – but this show’s important. This industry has no guard rails. You can’t sue them, you can’t do anything, so of course they’re going to take advantage of the population. That’s exactly what they’ve done. The destructive environmental impact alone is enough reason to take to the streets and protest. Sure, there’s all this darkness online but also, we’re going to take your water and electricity from you, too.”

Park blackmails his therapist – sorry, “performance psychologist” (played by Barry’s Sarah Goldberg) – into giving him insider-trading tips from her other powerful clients. The pair are soon engulfed in a scandal over fraudulent stock pumping. It’s a familiar-sounding storyline. “Elon got into trouble for market manipulation,” says Glatzer. “It’s like Duncan says in the show: ‘It’s not a felony in Silicon Valley, it’s good hustle.’ That’s the mentality here. Laws are for morons, not us.”

Real world echoes are everywhere in The Audacity. The search engine of choice is called Spookle (slogan: “You Agreed to This”). A corporation called Cupertino is a thinly veiled reference to Apple, while its mythical boss “Big Tim” nods to Tim Cook. Are any of Glatzer’s characters directly based on real-life figures? “The truth is, I don’t find any of them worthy of a three-dimensional character that could go the distance of multiple seasons,” says Glatzer. “They’re interesting enough for a film like The Social Reckoning but not much more.”

Indeed, Magnussen can currently be seen in The Social Reckoning as a Meta spin doctor. Is this his tech bro era? “AI is the most pressing issue of our time,” he says. “It affects our planet, our politics, our mental health, everything. Technology can do wonderful things but once it starts dividing us or swaying elections, it’s deeply damaging.”

“I don’t understand why people get on board with social media,” sighs Galifianakis. “We fed these machines for years. Now these machines are going to find us. I don’t believe the promises of AI because I don’t trust the people doing it.”

The Audacity’s protagonist has been described as “highly punchable”. Magnussen concurs: “You’ve seen these guys in front of Congress. They’re pretty fucking punchable.” An early episode includes a sequence at a Palo Alto fight club, where nerds whack each other with keyboards and strangle each other with cables. “That’s real!” laughs Magnussen. “The tech bro fight club is an actual thing.”

Despite the plentiful real-world parallels, Glatzer has never met a tech mogul. “That’s fine by me,” he says. “I don’t imagine the conversation would be anything other than stage-managed and dishonest. They have people workshopping their handshake and smile, so what am I going to get from that? But I have talked to a number of people who work in the tech world. The first thing they say is: ‘I’m not like that. That’s those other guys. I’m one of the good ones.’”
“Me too,” says Magnussen. “The response I get is: ‘I know that guy!’ It’s always someone else. You want to go: ‘No, it’s you. You’re that guy.’”

In America’s richest enclave, hi-tech goes hand-in-hand with hippy-dippy.
